signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Acute Abdomen.back: Permissive (hypotensive) resuscitation — give blood in preference to crystalloid and aim for a palpable radial pulse / just-adequate perfusion rather than a normal blood pressure until the bleeding is surgically controlled. Over-aggressive fluid dislodges clot and worsens haemorrhage.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Acute Abdomen.front: What is a 'damage-control' approach in an unstable surgical abdomen?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Acute Abdomen.back: When the patient is too unstable for a long operation, the surgeon does a rapid, limited procedure (control bleeding and contamination), stabilises the patient in ICU, then returns for definitive surgery later.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Acute Abdomen.front: How does large-bowel obstruction differ from small-bowel obstruction in urgency, and what is a closed loop?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Acute Abdomen.back: LBO (commonly obstructing colorectal cancer or sigmoid volvulus) is more dangerous when the ileocaecal valve is competent — a closed loop forms, caecal pressure rises and the caecum can perforate. Sigmoid volvulus shows a ‘coffee-bean’ sign and is often decompressed endoscopically; a competent-valve closed loop needs early surgery.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Acute Abdomen.front: Why examine the external genitalia in a boy or young man with lower abdominal pain?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Acute Abdomen.back: Testicular torsion can present as lower-abdominal / iliac-fossa pain (referred via T10) and is a time-critical, can’t-miss emergency — the testis must be untwisted within about 6 hours. Always examine the scrotum, just as you examine every hernial orifice.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What is ascites?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Free fluid in the peritoneal cavity — presenting with abdominal swelling, weight gain, an everted umbilicus and (when tense) breathlessness. It is one of the ‘fluid’ causes of abdominal distension.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: How is ascites detected on examination?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Shifting dullness: percuss to dullness in the flank, then roll the patient onto the opposite side — the previously dull flank becomes resonant as fluid redistributes. Add a fluid thrill in tense ascites (flank dullness, central resonance). Ultrasound confirms even small volumes.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What is the SAAG and how is it calculated?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back:
The serum-ascites albumin gradient = serum albumin − ascitic albumin (from samples taken the same day). It classifies ascites by mechanism:
  • ≥11 g/L = portal hypertension
  • <11 g/L = a non-portal cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What does a high SAAG (≥11 g/L) indicate, and what are its causes?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back:
Portal hypertension —
  • cirrhosis (commonest)
  • alcoholic hepatitis
  • cardiac (right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis)
  • and Budd-Chiari syndrome.
Cardiac ascites is high-SAAG but protein-rich.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What does a low SAAG (<11 g/L) indicate, and what are its causes?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back:
A non-portal cause —
  • peritoneal malignancy
  • TB peritonitis
  • pancreatic ascites
  • and nephrotic syndrome.
These raise the ascitic protein / albumin, narrowing the gradient.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: How is ascites graded (EASL)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back:
• Grade 1: mild, detectable only on ultrasound
  • Grade 2: moderate, symmetrical distension
  • Grade 3: large / tense ascites.
Grade guides management — tense (grade 3) ascites needs therapeutic paracentesis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What must be sent from every diagnostic ascitic tap?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Albumin (for the SAAG), a cell count and differential (neutrophils), cytology and culture; add protein, amylase (pancreatic) and triglyceride (chylous) as guided. Every new ascites is tapped.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) and how is it diagnosed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Infection of ascitic fluid without a surgical source, in cirrhotic ascites — presenting with fever, abdominal pain, or encephalopathy / deterioration. Diagnosed by an ascitic neutrophil count ≥250 cells/mm³.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: How is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis treated?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: IV antibiotics (e.g. cefotaxime) and IV albumin (which reduces hepatorenal syndrome and mortality); afterwards give secondary antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What are the commonest organisms in SBP?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Gut organisms — E. coli and Klebsiella (Gram-negatives), and Streptococci / Enterococci. It is usually a monomicrobial infection; polymicrobial growth suggests secondary (surgical) peritonitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: How is uncomplicated cirrhotic ascites managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Moderate sodium restriction (no-added-salt, ~80–120 mmol/day) and diuretics — spironolactone first-line, ± furosemide; treat the underlying liver disease (including alcohol cessation) and avoid nephrotoxins / NSAIDs. Fluid restriction is added only for significant hyponatraemia (Na <125).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: How is tense or refractory cirrhotic ascites managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Large-volume paracentesis with albumin cover (for taps >5 L, ~8 g per litre removed). Refractory ascites — no response to (or early recurrence despite) maximal diuretics + salt restriction, or diuretic-intractable due to complications — may need repeated LVP, a TIPS, or liver transplantation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: Why is IV albumin given with large-volume paracentesis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: To prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction (a fall in effective circulating volume → renal impairment and hyponatraemia). Albumin (~8 g per litre of ascites removed) is given when >5 L is drained.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What is the pathophysiology of cirrhotic ascites?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Portal hypertension → splanchnic vasodilatation and a fall in effective circulating volume → activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system with renal sodium and water retention; hypoalbuminaemia lowers oncotic pressure.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What is hepatorenal syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Functional renal failure in advanced cirrhosis / ascites from intense renal vasoconstriction (kidneys are structurally normal) — a diagnosis of exclusion. Precipitated by SBP, large-volume paracentesis without albumin, or GI bleeding; managed with terlipressin + albumin and transplant.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: How does malignant ascites present and how is it confirmed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: A low SAAG with weight loss from peritoneal carcinomatosis (ovarian, GI, breast); confirmed by positive cytology (note: ascites from massive hepatic metastases / HCC is high-SAAG). Palliate recurrent malignant ascites with therapeutic paracentesis or a tunnelled indwelling peritoneal drain, plus cancer treatment.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What are the features of TB peritonitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: A low-SAAG ascites with fever, night sweats and weight loss; the ascitic fluid shows lymphocytosis and a high adenosine deaminase (ADA). Diagnosis often needs peritoneal (laparoscopic) biopsy; treat with anti-TB therapy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What is chylous ascites?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Milky, triglyceride-rich ascitic fluid from lymphatic obstruction or disruption (lymphoma, malignancy, trauma / surgery, TB, cirrhosis) — the ascitic fluid has a high triglyceride level.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What is Budd-Chiari syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Hepatic venous outflow obstruction (hepatic-vein / IVC thrombosis) — presenting with the triad of abdominal pain, ascites (high SAAG) and tender hepatomegaly; associated with prothrombotic states (e.g. myeloproliferative disease). Diagnosed on Doppler ultrasound.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What is the first-line imaging to confirm ascites?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Ultrasound — it detects even small volumes of free fluid, characterises the liver, and guides paracentesis; CT is used to stage malignancy or find a non-portal cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What examination findings point to cirrhosis as the cause of ascites?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back:
• Peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, leukonychia, gynaecomastia, caput medusae)
  • jaundice
  • splenomegaly
  • and asterixis (encephalopathy)
— pointing to portal-hypertensive (high-SAAG) ascites.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What causes a high SAAG but protein-rich ascites, and why is it a trap?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Cardiac ascites (right heart failure / constrictive pericarditis) — the sinusoids are not damaged, so protein leaks across, giving a protein-rich but high-SAAG fluid. By the old protein classification it looks ‘exudative’, but the SAAG correctly identifies portal hypertension.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: How does cardiac ascites differ clinically from cirrhotic ascites?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: Cardiac ascites comes with a raised JVP, peripheral oedema and signs of heart failure (rather than liver stigmata); both are high-SAAG. An echocardiogram and treating the heart failure are key.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: Which drugs should be avoided in a patient with cirrhotic ascites?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: NSAIDs (precipitate renal impairment and diuretic resistance), ACE inhibitors / ARBs (hypotension, renal impairment) and nephrotoxins / aminoglycosides; use opioids and sedatives cautiously (encephalopathy risk).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What are the complications of ascites?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back:
• Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
  • hepatorenal syndrome
  • hyponatraemia
  • tense ascites with respiratory compromise
  • umbilical / paraumbilical hernia
  • and hepatic hydrothorax (a pleural effusion from fluid tracking through the diaphragm).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What is hepatic hydrothorax?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: A pleural effusion (usually right-sided) in a cirrhotic patient, from ascitic fluid tracking through diaphragmatic defects — it may occur with little apparent ascites and is managed like ascites (with treatment of the liver disease).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: Who should receive primary / secondary antibiotic prophylaxis against SBP?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back:
• Secondary: everyone after an episode of SBP.
  • Primary: cirrhotics with a low ascitic protein (<15 g/L) ± advanced disease, or during a GI bleed — usually a quinolone (ciprofloxacin).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What are the key complications of a TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: It relieves refractory ascites / variceal bleeding by lowering portal pressure, but commonly precipitates hepatic encephalopathy (~30–50%) and can worsen cardiac failure; it is contraindicated in severe encephalopathy or heart failure.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What is the units pitfall when calculating the SAAG?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: SAAG 11 g/L = 1.1 g/dL — the threshold is the same value in different units. Always subtract ascitic from serum albumin (not the reverse), and keep both samples in the same units, or the portal / non-portal classification flips.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.front: What are the caveats around non-selective beta-blockers and vasoconstrictors in advanced ascites?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Ascites.back: In refractory ascites, SBP or hypotension, non-selective beta-blockers may be harmful (the ‘window hypothesis’) and are often reduced / stopped. In hepatorenal syndrome, splanchnic vasoconstrictors — terlipressin (+ albumin), or midodrine (± octreotide) / noradrenaline — support renal perfusion.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: A ‘flapping tremor’ — brief, irregular lapses of posture (a negative myoclonus, i.e. sudden momentary loss of muscle tone), not a true rhythmic tremor. When bilateral it is a sign of metabolic encephalopathy; when unilateral it indicates a contralateral structural brain lesion.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: How do you elicit asterixis at the bedside?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Ask the patient to hold both arms out, dorsiflex the wrists (‘stop the traffic’) and spread the fingers, then watch for ~30 seconds — the hands flap forward as tone is briefly lost, then recover.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: Why is asterixis called a ‘negative myoclonus’?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Because it is caused by a brief lapse in the tonic muscle contraction holding a posture (a moment of EMG silence) — the drop and recovery of tone produce the flap, unlike a positive myoclonic jerk (a sudden muscle contraction).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: Why does asterixis disappear as a patient becomes comatose?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Because eliciting it needs the patient to actively sustain a posture. As consciousness falls they can no longer maintain the posture, so the flap is lost — its disappearance can signal deepening encephalopathy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: What is the significance of unilateral versus bilateral asterixis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Bilateral asterixis indicates a metabolic encephalopathy (hepatic, CO₂ retention, uraemia, drugs). Unilateral asterixis indicates a contralateral structural brain lesion (e.g. thalamic or internal-capsule stroke) — image the brain.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: What causes the asterixis of hepatic encephalopathy (‘liver flap’)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Chronic liver disease with hyperammonaemia and other neurotoxins that the failing liver cannot clear, producing a diffuse metabolic encephalopathy. Look for the stigmata of chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, spider naevi).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: Name common precipitants of hepatic encephalopathy to look for in a flapping cirrhotic patient.
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back:
• GI bleed
  • infection (especially SBP)
  • constipation
  • sedatives / opioids
  • electrolyte disturbance (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia)
  • dehydration / diuretics
  • and a high protein load.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: In which West Haven grade of hepatic encephalopathy is asterixis most prominent?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Grade II — lethargy / disorientation with obvious asterixis. (Grade I: mild, subtle changes; Grade III: marked confusion / somnolence; Grade IV: coma, when the flap is lost.)

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: Which respiratory problem causes asterixis, and what other signs accompany it?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Type 2 respiratory failure with CO₂ retention (CO₂ narcosis) — classically in COPD. Accompanying signs: bounding pulse, warm flushed peripheries, drowsiness and headache. Confirm with an ABG.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: How is renal disease a cause of asterixis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Uraemic encephalopathy in acute or chronic renal failure — retained uraemic toxins cause a metabolic encephalopathy. Check U&E (raised urea / creatinine).
Anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine, gabapentin, valproate), lithium, sedatives / benzodiazepines, and alcohol. Consider drug levels and a medication review in a flapping patient.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: Which inherited disorder should you consider in a young patient with asterixis, liver disease and neuropsychiatric signs?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Wilson’s disease (copper accumulation) — young patient with combined hepatic and neurological / psychiatric features; look for Kayser-Fleischer rings and a low serum caeruloplasmin.
Hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia — check glucose and electrolytes as part of the metabolic screen in any flapping patient.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: What investigations does a patient with BILATERAL asterixis need?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: A metabolic screen: LFTs + ammonia (hepatic), ABG (CO₂ retention), U&E (uraemia), glucose, K⁺, Mg²⁺, and drug levels; assess conscious level (GCS) and screen for a precipitant.
Urgent CT / MRI brain — unilateral asterixis reflects a contralateral structural lesion (e.g. thalamic or internal-capsule stroke), not a metabolic cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: How should you give oxygen to a drowsy COPD patient with asterixis and suspected CO₂ narcosis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Give controlled / titrated oxygen (target sats ~88–92%) guided by ABG — not uncontrolled high-flow, which can worsen hypercapnia. Treat the cause of decompensation and consider ventilatory support (e.g. NIV).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: How does asterixis differ from a true tremor on inspection of both hands?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Asterixis is irregular and bilaterally asynchronous (the two hands flap out of time) and it is a negative myoclonus (a lapse of tone) that appears only on a sustained posture — unlike a true tremor, which is a rhythmic, roughly symmetrical oscillation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.front: Besides the hands, where else can asterixis be seen?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Asterixis (Live.back: Wherever a posture is sustained — the dorsiflexed foot, protruded tongue, or closed eyelids. The wrists are simply the easiest site to demonstrate it.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What is caput medusae?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: A cluster of dilated, tortuous veins radiating from the umbilicus across the abdominal wall — named for the snake-like ‘head of Medusa’ appearance. It comes from recanalisation of the umbilical / paraumbilical veins and is a sign of portal hypertension (not an oestrogen effect).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What is the underlying cause of caput medusae?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: Portal hypertension — high portal pressure reopens the umbilical vein (via paraumbilical veins in the falciform ligament connecting to the left portal vein), shunting blood to systemic abdominal-wall veins around the umbilicus.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: How does the direction-of-flow test distinguish caput medusae from IVC obstruction?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: Empty a vein below the umbilicus and watch it refill. In portal hypertension (caput medusae) flow radiates away from the umbilicus (downward below it — the normal direction); in IVC obstruction the flow below the umbilicus is upward (reversed) to bypass the block.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: Why is caput medusae clinically important?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: It signals portal hypertension, so the patient is at risk of oesophageal / gastric varices and variceal bleeding — arrange upper GI endoscopy to screen for varices and manage the underlying liver disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What is the Cruveilhier-Baumgarten murmur?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: A venous hum heard at the umbilicus / epigastrium over a patent recanalised umbilical vein — a continuous murmur. The acquired form (cirrhotic portal hypertension) is the Cruveilhier-Baumgarten syndrome; the rarer congenital form (a patent umbilical vein with a hypoplastic portal vein) is Cruveilhier-Baumgarten disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What is the commonest cause of the portal hypertension underlying caput medusae?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: Cirrhosis (of any cause — alcohol, viral hepatitis, NAFLD) — the commonest (intrahepatic) cause of portal hypertension. Look for the other stigmata of chronic liver disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What are the pre-hepatic and post-hepatic causes of portal hypertension?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: Pre-hepatic: portal vein thrombosis (splenomegaly with a normal liver). Post-hepatic: Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic-vein outflow obstruction) and severe right heart failure / constrictive pericarditis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: Which other signs of portal hypertension accompany caput medusae?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: Ascites, splenomegaly, oesophageal / gastric varices, and (with chronic liver disease) spider naevi, palmar erythema and other stigmata; a venous hum may be audible.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: How is caput medusae confirmed and the cause investigated?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: Clinically (the flow test) plus ultrasound with Doppler (portal-vein patency and flow direction), LFTs / clotting / FBC, and CT / MR portography if needed; upper GI endoscopy screens for varices.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: How common is a true caput medusae, and how is it told from a thin person's veins?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: A true, florid caput medusae is relatively uncommon and late — more often you see dilated abdominal-wall veins. Distinguish it from the faint, non-dilated superficial veins of a thin person (which are not tortuous, carry normal flow, and lack other portal-hypertension signs).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: How do you distinguish caput medusae from the collaterals of IVC obstruction on inspection?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: Caput medusae radiates from the umbilicus (flow away from it). IVC obstruction gives dilated veins over the flanks / lateral abdominal wall carrying blood upward (below the umbilicus) toward the SVC territory.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What is the danger of the varices associated with caput medusae?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: Variceal haemorrhage — a life-threatening upper-GI bleed. Patients need screening endoscopy and primary prophylaxis (non-selective beta-blocker or endoscopic band ligation) once varices are found.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: Is caput medusae an oestrogen-mediated sign like spider naevi?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: No — unlike spider naevi and palmar erythema (oestrogen-mediated), caput medusae is a mechanical / haemodynamic sign of portal hypertension (portosystemic shunting).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What examination should accompany finding caput medusae?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back:
A full chronic-liver-disease and portal-hypertension examination:
  • ascites (shifting dullness)
  • splenomegaly
  • spider naevi
  • palmar erythema
  • jaundice
  • and signs of encephalopathy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What is portal hypertension, in terms of pressure?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: A pathological rise in the portal venous pressure gradient (the hepatic venous pressure gradient, HVPG); clinically significant portal hypertension is an HVPG ≥10 mmHg, and variceal bleeding risk rises above ~12 mmHg.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What are the four classic complications of portal hypertension?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back:
• Varices (oesophageal / gastric — bleeding)
  • ascites
  • splenomegaly with hypersplenism (cytopenias)
  • and hepatic encephalopathy (portosystemic shunting of toxins).
Caput medusae is one visible collateral of the same process.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What is hepatofugal flow and why does it matter in portal hypertension?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: Hepatofugal flow is portal-vein blood flowing away from the liver (reversed from the normal hepatopetal direction) — a Doppler marker of significant portal hypertension and the drive behind portosystemic collaterals such as caput medusae.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What is a globally important cause of portal hypertension besides cirrhosis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: Schistosomiasis — a leading cause of portal hypertension worldwide (periportal / ‘pipe-stem’ fibrosis) — giving splenomegaly and varices, often with relatively preserved liver function.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: How can portal hypertension / refractory varices be treated when medical therapy fails?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back: A TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) lowers portal pressure — used for refractory varices / ascites, but risks hepatic encephalopathy. Lowering portal pressure (TIPS or transplant) can make the collaterals / caput medusae regress; transplant is definitive for end-stage disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.front: What are the main sites of portosystemic collateral (varices) in portal hypertension?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Caput Medusae.back:
• Gastro-oesophageal junction (oesophageal / gastric varices — the dangerous ones)
  • the umbilicus (caput medusae)
  • the rectum (anorectal varices)
  • and the retroperitoneum.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What counts as a significant change in bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: A persistent change (usually >4–6 weeks) in stool frequency, consistency or form — new looser / more frequent motions, or new constipation — especially with red-flag features. It can be the first sign of colorectal cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What is the Bristol stool chart used for?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: It classifies stool form from type 1 (separate hard lumps) to type 7 (watery) — a standardised way to describe consistency. Types 1–2 suggest constipation; 6–7 suggest diarrhoea; 3–4 are ‘normal’.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What are the red-flag features suggesting colorectal cancer in a change of bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back:
• A persistent change to looser / more frequent stool (especially ≥60)
  • rectal bleeding
  • iron-deficiency anaemia
  • unexplained weight loss
  • an abdominal / rectal mass
  • or a positive FIT
— each triggers the suspected-cancer pathway.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What is the FIT (faecal immunochemical test) and how is it used?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: A stool test detecting human haemoglobin. It triages referral for suspected colorectal cancer — a positive FIT (≥10 µg Hb/g faeces) prompts an urgent (2-week-wait) colonoscopy. Crucially, a negative FIT does NOT exclude cancer — still refer if there is a mass, unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia or persistent concern.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: How does faecal calprotectin help in a change of bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: It is a marker of bowel inflammation — a raised calprotectin suggests inflammatory bowel disease, while a normal level supports a functional cause (IBS). It helps decide who needs colonoscopy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What are the NICE two-week-wait thresholds for suspected colorectal cancer?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back:
Refer urgently for:
  • ≥40 with abdominal pain + weight loss
  • ≥50 with unexplained rectal bleeding
  • ≥60 with iron-deficiency anaemia OR a change to looser / more frequent stool
  • a rectal or abdominal mass at any age
  • and use FIT to support referral in others who fall short of these.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: How is irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) characterised?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Abdominal pain (≥6 months) relieved by defecation, with bloating and altered bowel habit, and normal examination and investigations. It is a positive diagnosis made after excluding red flags (and checking coeliac serology / calprotectin).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What red flags make IBS unsafe to diagnose without investigation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back:
• Age ≥60 with a change in bowel habit (or ≥50 with rectal bleeding)
  • weight loss
  • iron-deficiency anaemia
  • a mass
  • nocturnal symptoms
  • or a family history of bowel cancer / IBD
— these mandate investigation before attributing symptoms to IBS.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: How does coeliac disease cause a change in bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Villous atrophy causes malabsorption — diarrhoea (or steatorrhoea), bloating, weight loss and iron / folate deficiency. Screen with anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-TTG) IgA plus total IgA (on a gluten-containing diet — a normal total IgA is needed because IgA deficiency gives a false-negative tTG); confirm with duodenal biopsy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: How does inflammatory bowel disease typically present as a change in bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Bloody diarrhoea, urgency and abdominal pain in a younger patient, often with weight loss and a raised faecal calprotectin / CRP. Colonoscopy with biopsy confirms Crohn’s or ulcerative colitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: How does diverticular disease affect bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: It can cause an altered bowel habit with left-iliac-fossa pain in an older patient; acute diverticulitis adds fever and raised inflammatory markers. It is a common cause but colorectal cancer must be excluded.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: When should Clostridioides difficile be suspected as a cause of diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: After recent antibiotics (especially broad-spectrum) or PPIs, in hospital or care-home patients — causing profuse diarrhoea ± colitis. Diagnose with a stool C. difficile toxin test.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: How does thyroid disease alter bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Hyperthyroidism speeds transit → diarrhoea / more frequent stool; hypothyroidism slows it → constipation. Check TFTs in an unexplained change of bowel habit.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: Which drugs commonly cause constipation, and which cause diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Constipation: opioids, iron, anticholinergics, calcium-channel blockers, calcium / aluminium antacids. Diarrhoea: antibiotics, metformin, PPIs, laxatives, NSAIDs, magnesium salts. Always review the drug chart.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What is the significance of nocturnal diarrhoea or symptoms waking the patient?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Nocturnal symptoms suggest an organic (not functional) cause — e.g. IBD, colorectal cancer or infection. IBS classically does not wake the patient from sleep, so this is a red flag.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What does new pencil-thin (ribbon-like) stool suggest?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: A narrowed rectal / distal colonic lumen — classically an obstructing colorectal cancer (or a stricture). It warrants investigation for malignancy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What is tenesmus and what does it suggest?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: A persistent sensation of incomplete evacuation / needing to pass stool despite an empty rectum — suggesting a rectal mass (cancer), proctitis or IBD. It is a localising red flag for rectal pathology.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: How can constipation paradoxically present as diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Overflow diarrhoea — liquid stool leaks around a faecal impaction (common in the elderly / immobile). A PR examination revealing a loaded rectum is the clue; treat the underlying constipation, not the ‘diarrhoea’.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: Which blood tests are useful in the work-up of a change in bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: FBC + ferritin (iron-deficiency anaemia), U&E, LFTs, TFTs, coeliac serology (anti-TTG), CRP and calcium — screening for malignancy, malabsorption, inflammation and systemic causes.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: Why is iron-deficiency anaemia a red flag in a change of bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: It suggests chronic occult GI blood loss — classically from a right-sided (caecal) colorectal cancer, which bleeds slowly without visible blood. Unexplained IDA mandates GI investigation (upper & lower).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What is bile-acid malabsorption?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Excess bile acids reaching the colon (e.g. after cholecystectomy, terminal-ileal Crohn’s / resection, or idiopathic) causing chronic watery diarrhoea. Diagnosed with a SeHCAT scan; treated with a bile-acid sequestrant (colestyramine).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: How does ischaemic colitis present as a change in bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Sudden crampy abdominal pain then bloody diarrhoea in an older patient with vascular risk factors — from reduced colonic perfusion (often the splenic flexure ‘watershed’). Usually managed supportively; imaging / colonoscopy confirm it.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: Which hereditary conditions raise colorectal-cancer risk and should prompt a family history?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) — ask about bowel cancer in relatives and the age at diagnosis; they change screening / referral thresholds.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What is the initial management once a functional (IBS) diagnosis is secure?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back:
• Reassurance and a positive diagnosis
  • dietary / lifestyle measures (e.g. fibre adjustment, low-FODMAP with dietitian)
  • symptom-directed drugs (antispasmodics, laxatives / loperamide)
  • and safety-netting to return if red flags develop.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: Why must a first presentation of 'IBS' in an older patient be treated with caution?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Because colorectal cancer becomes far more likely with age — a new change of bowel habit over 60 (or with any red flag) needs investigation (FIT / colonoscopy) before a functional label; IBS usually presents in younger adults.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What stool investigations are used in a change of bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back:
• FIT (occult blood → cancer pathway)
  • faecal calprotectin (IBD vs IBS)
  • and stool culture & C. difficile toxin (infection)
— chosen by the clinical picture.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What is microscopic colitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: A cause of chronic watery (non-bloody) diarrhoea, typically in older women, associated with NSAIDs / PPIs and autoimmune disease. The colonoscopy looks normal — the diagnosis is made on biopsy; treated by stopping culprit drugs ± budesonide.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What examination is essential in every change of bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: A digital rectal examination (PR) — for a rectal mass, blood, or a loaded rectum (impaction) — plus an abdominal examination for masses and organomegaly.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What does alternating constipation and diarrhoea suggest?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: It is common in IBS, but can also occur with an obstructing colorectal cancer (constipation with overflow) or diverticular disease — so red flags must still be excluded, especially in older patients.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What is the significance of mucus in the stool?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Mucus is common and often benign (IBS), but can accompany IBD, infection, or a rectal tumour / villous adenoma. It is assessed alongside the other features rather than in isolation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: How is a suspected malabsorptive cause of chronic diarrhoea investigated?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back:
• Coeliac serology (anti-TTG)
  • faecal elastase (pancreatic insufficiency)
  • consideration of bile-acid malabsorption (SeHCAT) and lactose intolerance
alongside nutritional bloods (ferritin, B12, folate, calcium).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: Why should calcium be checked in a change of bowel habit?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Hypercalcaemia causes constipation (‘bones, stones, groans, moans’) — and may itself signal malignancy or hyperparathyroidism. It is a simple, correctable systemic cause worth excluding.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.front: What is the role of colonoscopy versus CT colonography?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel.back: Colonoscopy is first-line (visualises + biopsies + removes polyps). CT colonography is used when colonoscopy is incomplete, high-risk or declined — it images the colon but cannot biopsy, so positive findings still need endoscopy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How is constipation defined?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back:
Infrequent (<3 stools per week) or difficult defecation —
  • hard / lumpy stool (Bristol 1–2)
  • straining
  • a sense of incomplete evacuation or blockage
  • and needing manual manoeuvres.
It is a symptom, not a single diagnosis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What is the difference between primary and secondary constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Primary (functional) constipation has no identifiable organic cause (normal-transit, slow-transit, or dyssynergic defecation). Secondary constipation is due to drugs, metabolic, mechanical or neurological causes — which must be excluded.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: Which drugs most commonly cause constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back:
• Opioids (the classic)
  • iron
  • anticholinergics (antimuscarinics, tricyclics, antipsychotics)
  • calcium-channel blockers (verapamil)
  • calcium / aluminium antacids and ondansetron
(diuretics only indirectly, via dehydration / hypokalaemia). Always review the drug chart.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: Which metabolic and endocrine disturbances cause constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back:
• Hypercalcaemia
  • hypothyroidism
  • hypokalaemia
  • diabetes (autonomic neuropathy) and pregnancy (progesterone).
Check calcium, TFTs and potassium in unexplained constipation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What are the red-flag features of constipation suggesting colorectal cancer?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back:
• New-onset constipation ≥60
  • PR bleeding
  • unexplained weight loss
  • iron-deficiency anaemia
  • an abdominal / rectal mass
  • or a positive FIT
— these mandate FIT / colonoscopy on the suspected-cancer pathway.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How does bowel obstruction present with constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Acute constipation with abdominal distension, vomiting and no flatus (absolute constipation), plus colicky pain — a surgical emergency needing NBM, IV fluids, an NG tube and imaging (AXR / CT).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What is cauda equina syndrome and why is it relevant to constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Compression of the cauda equina — presenting with constipation / urinary retention or incontinence, saddle anaesthesia, bilateral sciatica and reduced anal tone. It is an emergency needing urgent MRI and decompression.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What is overflow diarrhoea, and how does it relate to constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Liquid stool leaking around a faecal impaction — often mistaken for diarrhoea, especially in the elderly / immobile. A PR examination revealing a loaded rectum is the clue; treat the underlying constipation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What is faecal impaction and how is it managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: A large mass of hard stool the patient cannot pass (often with overflow). Treat with high-dose oral macrogol first; if that fails, suppositories / enemas; manual evacuation is a last resort.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How do bulk-forming laxatives work, and what is a key caution?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Ispaghula husk / methylcellulose increase stool bulk and retain water. They need adequate fluid intake, take days to work, and should be avoided in opioid-induced constipation and obstruction (risk of impaction / obstruction).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How do osmotic laxatives work, and give examples.
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: They draw water into the bowel lumen, softening stool and increasing frequency. Examples: macrogol (polyethylene glycol), lactulose and phosphate enemas. Macrogol is the usual first-line osmotic (added when a bulk-forming laxative is insufficient).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How do stimulant laxatives work, and give examples.
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: They stimulate colonic peristalsis. Examples: senna, bisacodyl, sodium picosulfate and glycerol suppositories. They act faster (6–12 h orally) and are useful for opioid-induced constipation (with an osmotic).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How is opioid-induced constipation managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Co-prescribe an osmotic + stimulant laxative (avoid bulk-forming, which can worsen it); if refractory, use a peripherally-acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist (PAMORA) such as naloxegol or methylnaltrexone.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What is the general laxative ladder for chronic constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Lifestyle (fibre, fluids, activity) → bulk-forming → add / switch to an osmotic (macrogol) → add a stimulant → suppositories / enemas; refractory cases may need prucalopride (a 5-HT₄ agonist).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What lifestyle measures are first-line for constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back:
• Increase dietary fibre gradually
  • increase fluid intake
  • and increase physical activity
with good toileting habits (responding to the urge, unhurried time, correct posture). These underpin all pharmacological treatment.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How does hypothyroidism cause constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Low thyroid hormone slows gut motility, causing constipation alongside fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain and dry skin. Check TFTs and treat with levothyroxine.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: Why does hypercalcaemia cause constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: High calcium reduces smooth-muscle / neuromuscular excitability, slowing the gut — part of ‘bones, stones, groans and moans’ (with polyuria, confusion and abdominal pain). Check calcium; it may signal malignancy or hyperparathyroidism.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How does hypokalaemia contribute to constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Low potassium impairs smooth-muscle contraction, slowing gut motility (and, if severe, causing ileus). Correct potassium — and remember diuretics and vomiting as causes.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What is Hirschsprung's disease?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: A congenital absence of ganglion cells (aganglionosis) in the distal colon — causing failure to pass meconium within 48 h and constipation / distension in a neonate / child. Diagnosed on rectal biopsy; treated surgically.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How does an anal fissure cause constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: The painful passage of hard stool leads to withholding (fear of defecation), which worsens constipation — a vicious cycle. Look for a posterior midline fissure and fresh blood on the paper; treat pain and soften stool.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How does Parkinson's disease affect the bowel?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Autonomic dysfunction and reduced mobility cause constipation, which is common and often precedes motor symptoms. Some anti-Parkinsonian and other drugs worsen it — manage with laxatives and activity.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What is dyssynergic defecation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: A failure to coordinate the pelvic-floor and anal-sphincter muscles during defecation (paradoxical contraction / inadequate relaxation) — causing difficulty and incomplete evacuation despite a normal-consistency stool. Treated with biofeedback.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: Which examination is essential in assessing constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: A digital rectal examination (PR) — for faecal impaction, a rectal mass, an anal fissure, and anal tone / sensation (the latter important in suspected cauda equina), plus an abdominal examination for masses.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: Which blood tests are useful in unexplained constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back:
• FBC (anaemia)
  • U&E (potassium)
  • calcium
  • TFTs and glucose
— to screen for the metabolic / endocrine causes and for anaemia suggesting malignancy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How do softener (surfactant) laxatives such as docusate work?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Docusate is a surfactant stool softener (with weak stimulant action) that lets water penetrate the stool. It is relatively weak — used as an adjunct or in faecal impaction rather than as a sole first-line agent.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: Why must you co-prescribe a laxative whenever starting an opioid?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Opioids reliably cause constipation (reduced motility and increased sphincter tone), and tolerance to this effect does not develop — so a stimulant ± osmotic laxative should be started prophylactically.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What is prucalopride and when is it used?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: A selective 5-HT₄ receptor agonist (prokinetic) used for chronic constipation that has not responded to at least two laxatives (from different classes) at adequate dose. It stimulates colonic motility.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What non-GI complication can straining at stool precipitate or worsen?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Straining raises intra-abdominal / venous pressure — worsening haemorrhoids and anal fissures, causing rectal prolapse, and (via a vasovagal / Valsalva effect) triggering syncope or cardiac events in vulnerable patients.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: How does the age and onset of constipation steer the work-up?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: New-onset constipation in an older patient is colorectal cancer until excluded (FIT / colonoscopy). Long-standing constipation from youth with no red flags is usually functional and managed with lifestyle and laxatives.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: Which laxative has a dual role in liver disease, and why?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Lactulose — besides treating constipation, it is used in hepatic encephalopathy because it acidifies the gut lumen and traps ammonia (as ammonium) and speeds its excretion, lowering blood ammonia.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What is the danger of using strong stimulant laxatives or enemas in suspected bowel obstruction?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: They can increase peristalsis / pressure against the obstruction, worsening pain and risking perforation. Suspected obstruction needs NBM, imaging and surgical assessment, not aggressive laxatives.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What features distinguish functional constipation / IBS-C from an organic cause?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Long-standing, stable symptoms with no red flags, a normal examination and normal bloods, often with pain relieved by defecation and bloating (IBS-C). Organic causes have red flags, recent onset, or abnormal tests.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: Why are older / immobile patients particularly prone to constipation and impaction?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Reduced mobility and fluid / fibre intake, multiple constipating drugs, comorbidity (e.g. Parkinson’s, hypothyroidism) and reduced rectal sensation combine — making constipation and faecal impaction with overflow common; a PR is essential.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.front: What is a caution with long-term stimulant laxative use?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation.back: Prolonged use of anthraquinone stimulants (e.g. senna) can cause melanosis coli (benign brown-black colonic pigmentation, reversible on stopping). Use stimulants intermittently / short-term where possible and avoid long-term dependence.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: A palpable, non-tender (enlarged) gallbladder in a patient with painless jaundice.
In a patient with painless jaundice and a palpable gallbladder, the cause is unlikely to be gallstones — so a malignant / other cause of biliary obstruction should be suspected.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: Why does Courvoisier's law hold — why can't chronic gallstones usually produce it?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: Chronic gallstone disease causes a fibrosed, shrunken, thick-walled gallbladder that cannot distend. A gallbladder that can enlarge implies obstruction from a different (usually malignant) cause distal to it.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: What is the commonest cause of Courvoisier's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas obstructing the distal common bile duct — the classic cause of painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: Besides pancreatic cancer, what malignant causes produce Courvoisier's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: Cholangiocarcinoma of the distal common bile duct and ampullary carcinoma (and, less often, duodenal tumours) — all obstruct the distal bile duct.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: What is the key clinical maxim linked to painless obstructive jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: Painless obstructive jaundice is malignancy until proven otherwise — it warrants urgent (2-week-wait) investigation for pancreatic / biliary cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: How does Courvoisier's sign differ from the palpable gallbladder of acute cholecystitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: In cholecystitis the gallbladder is palpable but TENDER, with a positive Murphy’s sign, and jaundice is usually absent. Courvoisier’s gallbladder is non-tender with painless jaundice.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: What are the features of the obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice seen with Courvoisier's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back:
• Dark urine (conjugated bilirubin in the urine)
  • pale stools (no bile reaching the gut)
  • pruritus
  • and a raised conjugated bilirubin.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: What LFT pattern is expected with Courvoisier's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: An obstructive (cholestatic) pattern: markedly raised ALP and GGT with a raised conjugated bilirubin, and comparatively modest transaminase rise.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: Which tumour marker is associated with pancreatic and biliary cancer?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: CA 19-9 — raised in pancreatic and biliary malignancy (to support diagnosis and monitor, not to screen). Caveats: it is falsely raised by obstructive jaundice / cholangitis and is undetectable in Lewis-antigen-negative people.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: What is the first-line imaging investigation for Courvoisier's sign, and what does it show?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: Abdominal ultrasound — showing a dilated common bile duct, a distended gallbladder and often a pancreatic head mass. It confirms the obstruction is distal.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: Which further imaging is used to characterise and stage the cause of Courvoisier's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back:
• CT pancreas (staging)
  • MRCP (biliary tree)
  • and endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with biopsy for tissue diagnosis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: How is the jaundice of a malignant biliary obstruction relieved, and what is the potential curative operation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: ERCP with biliary stenting relieves the jaundice (palliative or pre-op); a Whipple’s procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) is the potentially curative operation for a resectable pancreatic-head / ampullary / distal cholangiocarcinoma.
No — it is a rule of thumb. Rarely a common bile duct stone can cause a palpable gallbladder if it never became fibrosed. The teaching point (don’t assume gallstones) still stands.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: Which systemic features suggest pancreatic cancer in a patient with Courvoisier's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back:
• Weight loss, anorexia
  • new-onset diabetes
  • epigastric / back pain (late)
  • and migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau’s sign of malignancy).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: Why does a proximal (hilar / Klatskin) bile-duct tumour NOT produce Courvoisier's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: Because the obstruction is above the gallbladder / cystic-duct junction, so bile cannot back up to distend the gallbladder. Courvoisier’s sign needs a distal common bile duct obstruction, below that junction.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: At what anatomical level is the obstruction in Courvoisier's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: Distal to the gallbladder / cystic duct — at the distal common bile duct (e.g. compressed by a pancreatic-head mass), so bile backs up and distends the gallbladder.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.front: Why is the distinction between painful and painless jaundice clinically important here?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Courvoisier's S.back: Painful obstructive jaundice (with gallstones / fever) suggests stone disease or cholangitis; painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests malignancy — a different, urgent pathway.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How is diarrhoea defined?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: The passage of ≥3 loose or watery stools per day (or a persistent increase in stool looseness / frequency; >200 g/day). It is described by duration, character (watery / bloody / fatty) and mechanism.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How is diarrhoea classified by duration, and why does it matter?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back:
• Acute <2 weeks (usually infective and self-limiting)
  • persistent 2–4 weeks
  • and chronic >4 weeks (needs a work-up for organic disease).
Duration steers how aggressively you investigate.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What are the four mechanisms of diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back:
• Secretory (active fluid secretion)
  • osmotic (unabsorbed solute draws in water)
  • inflammatory (mucosal damage → blood / pus)
  • and malabsorptive (unabsorbed nutrients / fat).
Motility disorders are sometimes added.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How does a fasting test distinguish secretory from osmotic diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Secretory diarrhoea persists despite fasting (large-volume, watery — the prototype is cholera, ‘rice-water’ stool). Osmotic diarrhoea stops when the patient stops eating the offending solute (e.g. lactose, osmotic laxatives).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What is the commonest cause of acute diarrhoea, and its management?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Viral gastroenteritis (norovirus, rotavirus) — watery, self-limiting. Management is oral rehydration and supportive care; antibiotics are not indicated.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What is the commonest bacterial cause of gastroenteritis, and a key complication?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Campylobacter (often from undercooked poultry) — bloody diarrhoea, cramps and fever. It is associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: Why must antibiotics and antimotility agents be avoided in E. coli O157?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin producing) can cause haemolytic-uraemic syndrome (HUS) — and antibiotics and loperamide increase toxin exposure / HUS risk. Manage supportively; watch for falling Hb / platelets and AKI.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What is haemolytic-uraemic syndrome (HUS)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: A triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury, classically after E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin) diarrhoea in a child. Management is supportive (including dialysis if needed).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: When should Clostridioides difficile be suspected, and how is it diagnosed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: After recent antibiotics (esp. broad-spectrum) or PPIs, in hospital / care-home patients — watery diarrhoea ± colitis. Diagnose with a stool C. difficile toxin test; assess severity (WCC, creatinine, colitis).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How is C. difficile infection managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back:
• Stop the causative antibiotic
  • isolate (contact precautions, hand-washing with soap and water)
  • and give oral vancomycin first-line (NICE; oral fidaxomicin is the second-line alternative when vancomycin is ineffective, and the drug of choice for recurrence).
Consider faecal microbiota transplant for multiply-recurrent disease; severe / toxic megacolon needs surgical review.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What is traveller's diarrhoea and its usual cause?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Acute watery diarrhoea within days of travel, usually from enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC). It is mostly self-limiting (rehydrate); antibiotics (e.g. azithromycin / ciprofloxacin) are reserved for severe disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What features suggest Giardia as a cause of diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Persistent, non-bloody, foul-smelling greasy diarrhoea with bloating and flatulence after travel or contaminated water. Diagnosed on stool ova / cysts / parasites (or duodenal sampling); treated with metronidazole.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: Which organisms cause diarrhoea by a PREFORMED toxin, and how is the timing a clue?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus (the latter classically from reheated rice) — a preformed toxin causes rapid-onset (<6 hours) vomiting and diarrhoea, distinguishing it from organisms that must first colonise.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: Which infective causes classically produce BLOODY diarrhoea (dysentery)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Campylobacter, Shigella, E. coli O157 and Entamoeba histolytica (Salmonella can also be bloody) — invasive / cytotoxic organisms. Bloody diarrhoea also raises IBD and ischaemic colitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How do you assess the severity of diarrhoea at the bedside?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Assess dehydration (thirst, dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, hypotension, low urine output, confusion) and sepsis — guiding oral vs IV rehydration and admission.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What is oral rehydration therapy, and why does it work?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Oral rehydration salts (ORS) — a glucose-electrolyte solution that harnesses sodium-glucose co-transport (still active in secretory diarrhoea) to drive water absorption. It is first-line for mild-moderate dehydration.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: When are antibiotics indicated in acute infective diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Only for severe or systemic bacterial infection, specific organisms (e.g. C. difficile, Giardia, severe Shigella / Campylobacter, cholera), the immunocompromised or septic — guided by stool results. Most cases need none.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: In which situations must loperamide (an antimotility agent) be avoided?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: In bloody / inflammatory diarrhoea, suspected C. difficile, and E. coli O157 — slowing transit worsens toxin exposure and risks toxic megacolon / HUS. It is reasonable only in mild, non-bloody, non-infective-severe diarrhoea.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How does malabsorptive diarrhoea present, and what are the main causes?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back:
Steatorrhoea (pale, greasy, floating, offensive stool) with weight loss and nutritional deficiency. Causes:
  • coeliac disease
  • chronic pancreatitis (exocrine insufficiency)
  • bile-acid malabsorption
  • and small-bowel disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How does coeliac disease cause chronic diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Gluten-driven villous atrophy causes malabsorption — diarrhoea, bloating, weight loss and iron / folate deficiency. Screen with anti-TTG IgA (on gluten); confirm with duodenal biopsy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How does inflammatory bowel disease present as diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Chronic bloody diarrhoea with urgency, abdominal pain and weight loss in a younger patient, with a raised faecal calprotectin / CRP. Colonoscopy with biopsy confirms Crohn’s or ulcerative colitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What is microscopic colitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Chronic watery (non-bloody) diarrhoea, typically in older women, associated with NSAIDs / PPIs. The colonoscopy looks normal — the diagnosis is made on biopsy; treated by stopping culprit drugs ± budesonide.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How does hyperthyroidism cause diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Excess thyroid hormone increases gut motility → more frequent, looser stool, alongside weight loss (despite good appetite), tremor, heat intolerance and tachycardia. Check TFTs.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What is bile-acid malabsorption and how is it treated?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Excess bile acids reaching the colon (post-cholecystectomy, terminal-ileal Crohn’s / resection, or idiopathic) causing chronic watery diarrhoea. Diagnosed with a SeHCAT scan; treated with a bile-acid sequestrant (colestyramine).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How is chronic diarrhoea from IBS characterised?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Chronic diarrhoea (or alternating habit) with pain relieved by defecation and bloating, no red flags, and normal investigations (normal calprotectin, negative coeliac serology). It is a positive clinical diagnosis made after excluding red flags — not merely a diagnosis of exclusion.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: Which stool investigations are used in diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back:
• Stool culture (bacteria)
  • C. difficile toxin
  • ova, cysts & parasites (Giardia / amoebae)
  • faecal calprotectin (IBD vs IBS)
  • faecal elastase (pancreatic exocrine insufficiency) and FIT (occult blood / cancer)
— chosen by the picture.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: Which infections are notifiable / warrant public-health involvement?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Several — e.g. food poisoning, E. coli O157 / HUS, Salmonella, Shigella, cholera and typhoid. Notify the health-protection team and advise on hygiene and exclusion (e.g. food handlers, healthcare workers).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: Why can chronic diarrhoea cause hypokalaemia, and why does it matter?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Potassium is lost in the stool (and with dehydration-driven renal losses) — causing hypokalaemia (weakness, arrhythmia, ileus). Check and replace potassium in significant or prolonged diarrhoea.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What does the timing of onset after a meal suggest in food poisoning?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back:
• <6 hours → a preformed toxin (S. aureus, B. cereus)
  • ~8–16 hours → C. perfringens / B. cereus (diarrhoeal)
  • >16 hours → invasive / toxin-producing bacteria (Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: How should chronic diarrhoea in an older patient be approached?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: As a change in bowel habit — screen for colorectal-cancer red flags (FIT, weight loss, IDA, mass) and arrange colonoscopy; do not assume it is functional / infective without excluding malignancy and IBD.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What causes diarrhoea in an immunocompromised (e.g. HIV) patient that is unusual in the immunocompetent?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Cryptosporidium, CMV colitis, Microsporidium, Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) and severe / prolonged common infections — a lower threshold for stool studies, endoscopy and specialist input is needed.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: Why is a drug history essential in diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back:
Many drugs cause it —
  • antibiotics (and C. difficile)
  • metformin
  • PPIs
  • laxatives
  • magnesium salts
  • NSAIDs
  • colchicine and chemotherapy.
Stopping or switching the culprit often resolves it.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What is the danger of severe colitis (e.g. C. difficile or IBD) becoming toxic megacolon?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Toxic megacolon is colonic dilatation with systemic toxicity — risking perforation. Suspect it with a distended, tender abdomen and an unwell patient; it needs urgent imaging, medical therapy and surgical review.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What simple public-health advice reduces spread of infective diarrhoea?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Meticulous hand hygiene, and staying off work / school until 48 hours after the last episode (longer / specific rules for food handlers, healthcare workers and certain organisms). Avoid preparing food for others.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.front: What is enteric (typhoid) fever and how does it present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea.back: Systemic infection with Salmonella typhi / paratyphi in a returning traveller — fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain, rose spots, and constipation early then diarrhoea later. It is notifiable; diagnosed on blood culture and treated with antibiotics (ceftriaxone / azithromycin).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: A fibroproliferative disease of the palmar (and digital) fascia — progressive fibrosis producing nodules and cords and eventually a fixed flexion contracture of the fingers. It is a disease of the fascia, not the tendons.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: Which fingers and joints does Dupuytren's contracture most commonly affect?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: The ring (4th) and little (5th) fingers, drawing the MCP joints and then the PIP joints into fixed flexion. PIP involvement is harder to correct.
A painless palmar nodule (often at the base of the ring finger) → a palpable cord with skin puckering / tethering → a fixed flexion contracture of the finger.
Ask the patient to lay the palm flat on a table. If they cannot flatten the hand (the finger stays flexed) the test is positive — a marker of a functional contracture and a trigger to refer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: How do you distinguish Dupuytren's contracture from trigger finger?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: Dupuytren’s = a palmar-fascia cord with skin tethering and a passive fixed contracture. Trigger finger = a flexor-tendon nodule that catches / clicks on active movement, with no cord or skin tethering.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: How do you distinguish Dupuytren's contracture from an ulnar claw?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: An ulnar claw is neurological (ulnar nerve palsy) — the clawing corrects passively and there is sensory loss. Dupuytren’s is a fixed fascial cord that does not correct passively and has normal sensation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: Which liver-related factors are associated with Dupuytren's contracture?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: Alcohol excess and chronic liver disease — it is a recognised stigma of chronic liver disease; look for palmar erythema, leukonychia and other stigmata. However, most cases are idiopathic, so do not assume alcohol.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: How does diabetic Dupuytren's disease typically differ?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: It occurs in long-standing diabetes and is often milder and more radial-sided (middle and radial fingers) than the classic ulnar (ring / little finger) alcohol / idiopathic pattern.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: Which anti-epileptic drug is classically associated with Dupuytren's contracture?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: Phenytoin — long-term anticonvulsant (especially phenytoin) use is a recognised association.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: Which occupational exposures are linked to Dupuytren's contracture?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: Heavy manual labour, vibrating-tool use (hand-arm vibration syndrome) and repeated hand trauma. Smoking and HIV are further recognised risk factors.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: What is the commonest cause of Dupuytren's contracture?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: Idiopathic / hereditary disease — autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, in older men of Northern-European (‘Viking’) descent. It is a myth that most cases are due to alcohol.

An aggressive form with a higher recurrence risk, marked by:
  • young age of onset
  • bilateral disease
  • strong family history
  • and ectopic fibromatosis (knuckle pads / plantar / penile disease).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: What is ectopic Dupuytren's disease and give three examples.
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back:
Fibromatosis at sites outside the palm:
  • Garrod’s knuckle pads (over the dorsal PIP joints)
  • Ledderhose disease (plantar fascia)
  • and Peyronie’s disease (penile fascia).
They mark the diathesis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: What are the management options for Dupuytren's contracture?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: Observe if there is no functional limitation. For significant contracture: needle aponeurotomy or fasciectomy (surgical excision); collagenase injection is a recognised option but is not currently available in the UK. Recurrence is common with all options.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: What is the typical epidemiology / demographic of Dupuytren's contracture?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: Typically a painless condition of middle-aged and older men of Northern-European descent; it is frequently bilateral (around 40–50%). Onset before ~50 with bilateral disease suggests the aggressive diathesis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: How is Dupuytren's contracture diagnosed, and are investigations needed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: It is a clinical diagnosis — palpate the cord, note skin tethering and the passive contracture, and do the tabletop test. No imaging or blood tests are needed for the diagnosis itself; investigations are only to screen the associations (e.g. LFTs, HbA1c).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: What does skin puckering over a palmar cord indicate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back: Tethering of the skin to the diseased palmar fascia — a classic sign of Dupuytren’s that helps distinguish it from a tendon problem (tendon disease does not tether the skin).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.front: What are the main complications of surgery (fasciectomy) for Dupuytren's contracture?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dupuytren's Con.back:
• Digital nerve or artery injury
  • wound problems (sometimes needing a skin graft — dermofasciectomy)
  • stiffness
  • infection
  • and complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS).
These risks are why surgery is reserved for functional contractures, and recurrence remains common.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is dyspepsia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back:
A symptom complex of upper-GI origin —
  • epigastric pain or burning
  • postprandial fullness
  • early satiety
  • bloating
  • nausea
  • and belching.
It is a description, not a diagnosis; the job is to find the cause and screen for red flags.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What do the ALARMS red flags stand for in dyspepsia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back:
• Anaemia (iron-deficiency)
  • Loss of weight
  • Anorexia
  • Recent-onset progressive symptoms
  • Melaena / haematemesis (or epigastric mass)
  • Swallowing difficulty (dysphagia)
— each is a red flag prompting urgent endoscopy. (Bare age ≥55 with new dyspepsia but no red flags warrants routine endoscopy.)

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What are the NICE criteria for an URGENT (2-week-wait) upper-GI endoscopy?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Dysphagia at any age, or age ≥55 with weight loss AND upper-abdominal pain / reflux / dyspepsia. Also refer urgently for an upper-abdominal mass consistent with gastric cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is the primary-care pathway for dyspepsia WITHOUT red flags?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Review drugs and lifestyle, then either test for H. pylori and eradicate if positive, or a 4-week trial of a full-dose PPI (“test-and-treat”). Endoscopy is reserved for red flags or failure to respond.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: How is H. pylori tested for, and what must you do before testing?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: A urea breath test or stool antigen test. Stop the PPI for at least 2 weeks (and antibiotics for 4 weeks) beforehand, as they suppress the organism and cause false negatives.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is first-line H. pylori eradication therapy?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Triple therapy for 7 days: a PPI plus two antibiotics — typically amoxicillin + clarithromycin; if penicillin-allergic, use PPI + clarithromycin + metronidazole (amoxicillin is the drug dropped).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: How can the timing of pain with food distinguish a duodenal from a gastric ulcer?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Duodenal ulcer pain is classically relieved by food and worse when hungry / at night. Gastric ulcer pain is typically worse with food (and may be associated with weight loss / food avoidance).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What are the two main causes of peptic ulcer disease?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID / aspirin use — between them they account for the great majority. Rarer causes include Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and stress ulceration.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is functional (non-ulcer) dyspepsia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Chronic dyspepsia with a normal endoscopy and no identifiable organic cause — a diagnosis of exclusion. It is common; managed with reassurance, lifestyle change, H. pylori eradication and acid suppression / prokinetics.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: Which cardiac diagnosis must never be missed in a patient with 'indigestion'?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: An inferior myocardial infarction (or angina), which can present with epigastric discomfort, nausea and sweating — do an ECG in any patient where the pain could be cardiac (exertional, risk factors).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: Which drugs commonly cause dyspepsia / peptic ulceration?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: NSAIDs and aspirin (inhibit protective prostaglandins), plus steroids, bisphosphonates, SSRIs and potassium supplements. Always review the drug chart and stop or add gastroprotection.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is the significance of NEW dyspepsia in a patient 55 or over?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: It raises the concern of gastric or oesophageal cancer — new, persistent dyspepsia at ≥55 (especially with any ALARMS feature) warrants endoscopy rather than empirical treatment alone.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: How does gastric cancer typically present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: New dyspepsia with weight loss, anorexia, early satiety and iron-deficiency anaemia, often in an older patient; sometimes an epigastric mass or Virchow’s node. Diagnosed at endoscopy with biopsy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is Barrett's oesophagus and why does it matter?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Metaplasia of the lower oesophagus from squamous to columnar epithelium due to chronic acid reflux — a premalignant change that increases the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma; it needs surveillance.
