signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: How does the pain of pancreatic disease differ from typical dyspepsia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Epigastric pain radiating through to the back, often relieved by sitting forward — seen in pancreatitis, and in pancreatic cancer which may also cause painless jaundice and weight loss.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: How does biliary pain present, and how is it confirmed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Epigastric / RUQ pain after fatty food, which may radiate to the right scapula — from gallstones (biliary colic / cholecystitis). Confirmed on ultrasound.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: Which gastrointestinal condition should be excluded with serology in dyspepsia with bloating and altered bowels?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Coeliac disease — check anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-TTG) IgA antibodies (with total IgA to exclude deficiency) while the patient is on a gluten-containing diet; confirm with duodenal biopsy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What lifestyle measures help dyspepsia and GORD?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back:
• Weight loss
  • smaller and earlier meals
  • reducing alcohol / caffeine / fatty foods
  • stopping smoking
  • and raising the head of the bed for nocturnal reflux
— alongside reviewing culprit drugs.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What are the major complications of peptic ulcer disease?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back:
• Bleeding (haematemesis / melaena)
  • perforation (peritonitis, free air)
  • and gastric outlet obstruction (from chronic scarring)
— and, for gastric ulcers, the small risk of underlying malignancy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: Why should a gastric ulcer found at endoscopy be re-scoped, but not usually a duodenal ulcer?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Gastric ulcers can be malignant, so they are biopsied and re-endoscoped at 6–8 weeks to confirm healing and exclude cancer. Duodenal ulcers are almost never malignant and do not need routine repeat scoping.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: A gastrin-secreting tumour (gastrinoma) causing excess acid and multiple / recurrent / refractory peptic ulcers (often distal duodenum), with diarrhoea. Suspect it with ulcers resistant to treatment or in atypical sites; check fasting gastrin.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: How is a proven H. pylori-positive peptic ulcer managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Eradication therapy (PPI + two antibiotics for 7 days), stop NSAIDs, and continue a PPI to heal the ulcer; confirm eradication with a urea breath test (at least 4 weeks after treatment).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: How do PPIs and H2-receptor antagonists differ in mechanism?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: PPIs (e.g. omeprazole) irreversibly block the gastric H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump — the most potent acid suppression. H₂-antagonists (e.g. ranitidine historically, famotidine) block histamine-driven acid secretion and are weaker.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What features help distinguish cardiac from gastro-oesophageal epigastric pain?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Cardiac pain is more likely exertional, radiating to the arm / jaw, with sweating, breathlessness and ECG changes. Gastro-oesophageal pain relates to food and posture, with heartburn / acid regurgitation. Overlap is common — when in doubt, ECG and troponin first.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What symptoms define reflux-type versus dysmotility-type dyspepsia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back:
• Reflux-type: heartburn and acid regurgitation (GORD)
  • Dysmotility-type: postprandial fullness, early satiety, bloating and nausea
  • Ulcer-type: localised epigastric pain.
The pattern guides initial treatment.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is the risk of long-term untreated GORD?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Chronic reflux can cause oesophagitis, peptic strictures, and Barrett’s oesophagus (with its risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma) — which is why persistent or alarm-feature reflux is investigated.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: Why is iron-deficiency anaemia an alarm feature in dyspepsia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: It suggests chronic occult GI blood loss — e.g. from a gastric cancer or a bleeding ulcer — and mandates endoscopic investigation (upper ± lower GI).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: When should endoscopy come before a trial of acid suppression?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: When there are ALARMS red flags (or dysphagia), because a PPI can partially mask symptoms and delay a cancer diagnosis. Age ≥55 with persistent new dyspepsia should also be scoped (routinely) before committing to long-term acid suppression.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is the classic presentation of pancreatic cancer causing epigastric symptoms?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: Painless obstructive jaundice (often with a palpable gallbladder — Courvoisier’s law), or epigastric pain radiating to the back with weight loss. New-onset diabetes in an older patient is another clue.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What non-invasive test confirms H. pylori eradication after treatment?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: A urea breath test performed at least 4 weeks after finishing antibiotics and 2 weeks off the PPI. Stool antigen is an alternative; serology cannot confirm eradication (it stays positive).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is the mechanism by which NSAIDs cause peptic ulcers?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: They inhibit COX-1, reducing protective gastric prostaglandins (which maintain mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow) — leaving the mucosa vulnerable to acid. Co-prescribe a PPI if NSAIDs are unavoidable.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What is the link between H. pylori and gastric MALT lymphoma?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back: H. pylori drives most gastric MALT lymphoma (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) — and in early / localised disease, H. pylori eradication alone can induce regression of the lymphoma. It is another reason to find and treat the organism.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.front: What are the recognised adverse effects of long-term PPI use?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epi.back:
• Hypomagnesaemia
  • low vitamin B12
  • increased C. difficile / enteric infection risk
  • osteoporosis / fractures
  • hyponatraemia
  • and rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping.
Use the lowest effective dose and review the ongoing need.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is dysphagia, and why is it always taken seriously?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Difficulty swallowing. It is a red-flag symptom until proven benign because it may signal oesophageal / gastric cancer, and because an unsafe swallow risks aspiration.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: How do you distinguish oropharyngeal from oesophageal dysphagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Oropharyngeal (high): difficulty initiating the swallow, with coughing / choking, nasal regurgitation, drooling and a wet voice (usually neuromuscular). Oesophageal (low): food sticks a few seconds after swallowing, felt retrosternally.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: For oesophageal dysphagia, what does the pattern of solids vs liquids tell you?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Solids first, then liquids, and progressive = a mechanical (obstructing) lesion (cancer, stricture, ring). Solids AND liquids from the outset (often intermittent) = a motility disorder (achalasia, spasm, systemic sclerosis).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is the classic presentation of oesophageal cancer?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids) with weight loss, usually in an older patient; sometimes odynophagia, anaemia or hoarseness. Diagnosed at OGD with biopsy; staged with CT / EUS.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What are the main risk factors for the two types of oesophageal cancer?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Adenocarcinoma (lower third): GORD and Barrett’s oesophagus, obesity. Squamous-cell carcinoma (upper two-thirds): smoking and alcohol (also achalasia, Plummer-Vinson).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is a peptic stricture and how does it present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: A fibrotic narrowing of the lower oesophagus from chronic acid reflux, causing progressive dysphagia to solids on a background of long-standing GORD. Needs OGD (exclude cancer) and endoscopic dilatation plus a PPI.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is achalasia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back:
A motility disorder from failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax (loss of myenteric plexus neurons), causing
  • dysphagia to solids AND liquids
  • regurgitation of undigested food
  • and weight loss.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is the classic barium-swallow finding in achalasia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: A dilated oesophagus tapering to a ‘bird’s-beak’ at the gastro-oesophageal junction. Manometry confirms it (absent peristalsis, failure of LOS relaxation) and is the gold standard.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: How is achalasia managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Pneumatic balloon dilatation or surgical (Heller) myotomy ± fundoplication; botulinum toxin injection for those unfit for these. It also carries a small increased risk of oesophageal (squamous) cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is diffuse oesophageal spasm?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: A motility disorder of uncoordinated oesophageal contractions, causing intermittent dysphagia (solids and liquids) with retrosternal chest pain. Barium may show a ‘corkscrew’ oesophagus.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: How does systemic sclerosis affect swallowing?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: It causes smooth-muscle atrophy / fibrosis of the oesophagus with reduced peristalsis and a weak LOS — giving dysphagia and severe reflux. Look for Raynaud’s and tight, thickened skin.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is a pharyngeal (Zenker's) pouch and how does it present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: A posterior pharyngeal mucosal outpouching (through Killian’s dehiscence), typically in an older man, with regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, a neck gurgle and cough. Diagnosed on barium swallow.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: Why should endoscopy be avoided as the first test if a pharyngeal pouch is suspected?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: The endoscope can enter and perforate the pouch. Do a barium swallow first to demonstrate it; endoscopy (if needed) is then performed with care.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is a Schatzki ring?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: A thin mucosal ring at the gastro-oesophageal junction causing intermittent dysphagia to solids (classically a bolus of meat — ‘steakhouse syndrome’). Treated with endoscopic dilatation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Brown-Kelly) syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: The triad of iron-deficiency anaemia, dysphagia and a post-cricoid oesophageal web. It is premalignant (risk of post-cricoid squamous carcinoma); treat with iron replacement and dilatation of the web.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is the commonest neurological cause of oropharyngeal dysphagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Stroke — swallow assessment is a core part of acute stroke care, and an unsafe swallow means NBM until SALT review to prevent aspiration pneumonia.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: How does myasthenia gravis cause dysphagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Fatigable weakness of the bulbar muscles gives dysphagia that worsens through a meal / by the end of the day, often with ptosis, diplopia and a nasal voice. Confirmed with anti-AChR antibodies.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is the difference between bulbar and pseudobulbar palsy?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Both cause dysphagia and dysarthria. Bulbar palsy is a lower motor neurone lesion (flaccid, wasted / fasciculating tongue, absent jaw jerk). Pseudobulbar palsy is upper motor neurone (spastic tongue, brisk jaw jerk, emotional lability).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: How does motor neurone disease present with dysphagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Progressive bulbar involvement with tongue wasting and fasciculation, a mix of UMN and LMN signs, and no sensory loss. Aspiration is a major risk and a common terminal event.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is odynophagia, and what causes it?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back:
Pain on swallowing. Causes:
  • infective oesophagitis (Candida in the immunocompromised / inhaled-steroid users; HSV, CMV)
  • pill oesophagitis (bisphosphonates, doxycycline, NSAIDs)
  • severe reflux oesophagitis
  • and ulcerating tumours.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is the first-line investigation for oesophageal dysphagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Upper-GI endoscopy (OGD) — it visualises the mucosa and allows biopsy of any lesion; it is performed urgently when there are red flags. CT / EUS are used to stage cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: Which investigation confirms achalasia, and what must be done first?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Oesophageal manometry (the gold standard) confirms achalasia — absent peristalsis and failure of LOS relaxation; a barium swallow shows the bird-beak. But OGD is done first to exclude a GOJ malignancy mimicking achalasia (pseudoachalasia), especially in older patients.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is the appropriate investigation for oropharyngeal / neurological dysphagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: A videofluoroscopy (modified barium swallow) assessed with speech and language therapy (SALT) — it shows the swallow mechanism and aspiration in real time.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is the immediate priority in a patient with an unsafe swallow?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back:
• Keep the patient nil by mouth (NBM) to prevent aspiration
  • refer to SALT for a swallow assessment
  • and plan alternative nutrition (NG tube, or PEG if long-term).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What features of a swallow suggest it is unsafe (aspiration risk)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back:
• Coughing or choking on eating / drinking
  • a wet or gurgly voice after swallowing
  • drooling
  • and recurrent chest infections
— all signal aspiration and warrant NBM + SALT.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: How does the sensation of a 'lump in the throat' with normal swallowing differ from true dysphagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: That is globus sensation — a constant lump-in-the-throat feeling between meals with normal swallowing, often benign (reflux / anxiety). True dysphagia (food actually sticking, especially progressive) is a red flag.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: Why must new-onset dysphagia in an older patient be investigated urgently?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Because oesophageal / gastric cancer is a leading cause — new dysphagia (any age) warrants urgent (2-week-wait) endoscopy, and progression to liquids with weight loss makes malignancy likely.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is eosinophilic oesophagitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: An allergic / atopic inflammatory disorder of the oesophagus, classically in a young atopic man, causing dysphagia to solids and recurrent food-bolus impaction. OGD shows rings, furrows and white exudates; diagnosis is on biopsy (dense eosinophils); treat with a PPI or swallowed topical steroids and dietary / allergen measures.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What extrinsic (outside-the-oesophagus) lesions can cause dysphagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back:
• Mediastinal masses (lung cancer, lymphoma)
  • a retrosternal goitre
  • a massively enlarged left atrium
  • and a thoracic aortic aneurysm
— compressing the oesophagus from outside.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: How does the management of a swallow differ between a stroke and a progressive neuromuscular disease?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: In stroke the swallow may recover, so support (NBM, SALT, NG feeding) is often temporary. In progressive disease (MND, advanced Parkinson’s) dysphagia is usually irreversible — consider PEG feeding and advance-care planning.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What is the major complication shared by all causes of an unsafe swallow?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Aspiration pneumonia (and, acutely, airway obstruction / choking) — the reason a swallow assessment, NBM if unsafe, and SALT input are central to managing any dysphagia.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: How is an acute food-bolus obstruction of the oesophagus managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: Food-bolus impaction (food stuck, unable to swallow even saliva, drooling) needs urgent endoscopic disimpaction if it does not pass spontaneously. Afterwards, investigate the underlying cause — a stricture, Schatzki ring, or eosinophilic oesophagitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.front: What does progressive dysphagia with a hoarse voice suggest?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia.back: An oesophageal (or laryngeal) cancer invading / compressing the recurrent laryngeal nerve — hoarseness plus progressive dysphagia and weight loss is an ominous combination needing urgent investigation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: Periumbilical bruising (bluish ecchymosis around the umbilicus) — caused by blood from a retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal haemorrhage tracking to the skin.
Flank bruising (bluish ecchymosis of the loins) — caused by blood from a retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracking along fascial planes to the flank skin.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: What is the common mechanism of Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: Retroperitoneal / intra-abdominal haemorrhage that dissects along fascial planes to reach the subcutaneous tissue of the periumbilical region (Cullen’s) or flank (Grey Turner’s).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: How quickly do Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs appear, and what does this mean clinically?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: They are delayed, developing over 24–48 hours (or more). Because they are late and insensitive, their absence does not exclude a significant bleed — never wait for them.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: What condition are Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs classically associated with?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: Severe acute (haemorrhagic / necrotising) pancreatitis — where they are a marker of severity and poor prognosis, though they occur in only a small minority of cases.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: Are Cullen's and Grey Turner's signs sensitive or specific for pancreatitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: Neither — they are uncommon (low sensitivity) and occur in any cause of retroperitoneal / intra-abdominal bleeding (low specificity). They flag a significant bleed, not a specific disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: Which vascular emergency must always be excluded in a patient with flank/periumbilical bruising and shock?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: A ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) — a retroperitoneal bleed presenting with back / flank pain, a pulsatile mass and collapse; it is the must-not-miss vascular killer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: In a woman of childbearing age with these signs, what diagnosis and test are essential?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy causing intraperitoneal haemorrhage — do a β-hCG (and transvaginal ultrasound) before attributing the bleed to anything else.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: How can trauma cause Cullen's / Grey Turner's signs?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: Blunt abdominal trauma causing splenic or hepatic rupture, or other intra-abdominal / retroperitoneal bleeding, tracks to the skin as flank or periumbilical bruising.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: Which drug and haematological problems can cause spontaneous retroperitoneal bleeding with these signs?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: Anticoagulation (warfarin, DOACs, heparin) and bleeding disorders / coagulopathy, including DIC — producing spontaneous retroperitoneal or rectus-sheath haemorrhage.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: What is the immediate management of a shocked patient with Cullen's / Grey Turner's signs?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back:
ABCDE with major-haemorrhage resuscitation:
  • wide-bore IV access
  • crossmatch / activate the massive transfusion protocol
  • and urgent identification and control of the bleeding source.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: What is the imaging investigation of choice to locate the source of bleeding in a stable patient?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast — it localises the haemorrhage (pancreatitis, AAA, splenic injury, retroperitoneal bleed). A bedside FAST / ultrasound is used in the unstable or trauma patient.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: Which blood tests are important when Cullen's / Grey Turner's signs are found?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back:
• FBC
  • clotting screen
  • group & save / crossmatch
  • amylase / lipase (pancreatitis)
  • U&E
  • and a β-hCG in women of childbearing age.
The Glasgow (modified Glasgow / Imrie) and APACHE II scores (and Ranson’s); Cullen’s / Grey Turner’s signs are additional clinical markers of severe disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: What is a rectus sheath haematoma and how does it relate to these signs?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: Bleeding into the rectus abdominis sheath (often from anticoagulation or coughing straining), which can produce periumbilical / abdominal-wall bruising and mimic an intra-abdominal cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: Give a simple way to remember which sign is which.
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: Cullen’s = Central (peri-umbilical); Grey Turner’s = flank (‘turn to the side’). Both mean blood in the retroperitoneum / peritoneum tracking to the skin.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: Besides pancreatitis and ruptured AAA, name other causes of retroperitoneal/intra-abdominal haemorrhage giving these signs.
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back:
• Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
  • splenic / hepatic rupture
  • a ruptured visceral (e.g. splenic) artery aneurysm
  • a ruptured haemorrhagic ovarian cyst
  • and coagulopathy / anticoagulation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.front: When Cullen's or Grey Turner's sign appears in acute pancreatitis, what does it imply about outcome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Grey Turner's &.back: It signifies severe / necrotising pancreatitis with a markedly increased mortality (historically around a third of cases) — an adverse prognostic marker, though present in only a minority.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: How do you approach a groin lump?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: By two questions: is it a hernia? (cough impulse, reducibility) and where is it relative to the pubic tubercle? (above & medial → inguinal; below & lateral → femoral). Then read the character (pulsatile, disappears on lying, transilluminates) and screen for strangulation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: How are inguinal and femoral hernias distinguished at the bedside?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: By their relation to the pubic tubercle: an inguinal hernia lies above and medial; a femoral hernia lies below and lateral. Femoral hernias are commoner in women and have a higher strangulation risk.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is the difference between a direct and an indirect inguinal hernia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: An indirect hernia passes through the deep (internal) ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels (and can reach the scrotum); a direct hernia pushes through a weak posterior wall medial to the vessels. Indirect is commoner; the ring-occlusion test is unreliable.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What are the signs of a strangulated hernia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A tender, irreducible, tense lump with no cough impulse, often with overlying skin changes and features of bowel obstruction (colic, vomiting, distension). It is a surgical emergency — the blood supply is compromised.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: Why are femoral hernias repaired promptly even when asymptomatic?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: Because the narrow, rigid femoral canal gives femoral hernias a high risk of strangulation; they are repaired promptly (unlike small, asymptomatic inguinal hernias, where watchful waiting can be reasonable).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is the difference between a reducible, an incarcerated and a strangulated hernia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back:
• Reducible: contents return (cough impulse present)
  • incarcerated (irreducible): contents will not reduce but are viable
  • strangulated: the blood supply is cut off — tender, tense, no cough impulse — needing urgent surgery.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is a saphena varix and how is it recognised?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A dilatation of the saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction — a soft, bluish groin lump that disappears on lying down, has a cough impulse / palpable thrill, and comes with varicose veins. It can be mistaken for a femoral hernia.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: How do you recognise a femoral artery aneurysm as a groin lump?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A pulsatile, expansile lump over the femoral artery (it pushes the fingers apart). Never incise a pulsatile groin lump as a ‘hernia’; confirm with ultrasound / duplex.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is a femoral (false) pseudoaneurysm?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A pulsatile swelling after femoral arterial puncture / catheterisation (a contained leak), often with a bruit — confirmed on duplex ultrasound; managed by compression, thrombin injection or surgery.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is the differential of inguinal lymphadenopathy?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back:
• Infection (leg / foot, perineum, sexually transmitted infection)
  • malignancy (metastatic from the leg, anal canal, vulva / penis, or lymphoma)
— examine the drainage areas and the other node groups.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: How does an undescended or ectopic testis present as a groin lump?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A groin lump with an empty scrotum on that side — commonly in a child or young man. An undescended testis carries a raised risk of testicular cancer and infertility and needs urological referral (orchidopexy).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is a psoas abscess and how may it present in the groin?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A collection in the psoas sheath tracking to the groin — a fluctuant swelling below the inguinal ligament; the patient holds the hip flexed and pain is provoked on hip extension (a positive psoas sign), with back pain and systemic upset. Causes: TB (cold abscess), Crohn’s and spinal / discitis infection.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: Which groin lumps transilluminate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: Fluid-filled lumps — a hydrocele of the cord (or an encysted hydrocele) transilluminates; solid lumps (nodes, hernia contents, tumour) do not. Combine with the cough impulse and pulsatility to localise.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: How should a groin lump be examined?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back:
• Inspect and palpate standing and lying
  • find the pubic tubercle and the lump’s relation to it
  • test the cough impulse and reducibility, pulsatility and transillumination
  • examine the scrotum, abdomen and regional nodes, and auscultate.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: Why must the scrotum be examined in a patient with a groin lump?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: To see whether an inguinoscrotal hernia extends into it (you cannot get above such a lump), to detect an empty scrotum (undescended testis), and to distinguish a scrotal from a groin swelling.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: Is imaging needed to diagnose a groin hernia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: Usually no — most groin hernias are a clinical diagnosis. Ultrasound helps for an uncertain lump, a suspected occult hernia, a vascular lesion or a node; CT / MRI is reserved for occult or complex cases and psoas abscess.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is the difference between the mid-inguinal point and the midpoint of the inguinal ligament?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: The mid-inguinal point (midway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis) overlies the femoral artery; the midpoint of the inguinal ligament (midway between the ASIS and the pubic tubercle) overlies the deep inguinal ring — a classic viva distinction.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is the first-aid management of a suspected strangulated hernia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: Treat as a surgical emergency: nil by mouth, IV fluids, analgesia, an NG tube if obstructed, bloods and urgent surgical review for emergency repair. Do not force reduction of a tender, tense hernia.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: How does a hydrocele of the cord differ from a hernia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A hydrocele of the cord is a fluid-filled, transilluminable swelling along the spermatic cord that does not have a cough impulse and does not reduce into the abdomen; a hernia has a cough impulse and reduces.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is a Richter's hernia and why is it dangerous?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A hernia in which only part of the bowel wall (the antimesenteric border) is trapped — it can strangulate and perforate without causing complete obstruction, so the classic obstructive signs may be absent, delaying diagnosis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What structures make up the boundaries used to locate hernias (the pubic tubercle and inguinal ligament)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: The inguinal ligament runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle; inguinal hernias emerge above it (and above & medial to the tubercle), while femoral hernias emerge below it (below & lateral to the tubercle).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What are the borders of Hesselbach's triangle and its significance?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back:
• Medially the rectus sheath
  • laterally the inferior epigastric vessels
  • inferiorly the inguinal ligament.
A direct inguinal hernia pushes through this weak area of the posterior wall (medial to the vessels).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What does the spermatic cord (or round ligament) run through, and why does it matter?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: The inguinal canal — from the deep to the superficial ring. An indirect hernia follows the cord through the deep ring (so it can descend into the scrotum / labium); this anatomy underlies inguinoscrotal hernias.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is a sliding hernia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A hernia where a retroperitoneal organ (e.g. sigmoid colon, caecum or bladder) forms part of the wall of the sac itself — important surgically because the ‘sac’ contains bowel wall that must not be opened / damaged.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is a Littre's hernia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A hernia sac containing a Meckel’s diverticulum — it can strangulate; a named eponym worth recognising alongside Richter’s (partial bowel-wall) hernia.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is an obturator hernia and its classic sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A rare hernia through the obturator canal, typically in thin, elderly women, presenting with bowel obstruction and medial thigh / knee pain on internal rotation (the Howship-Romberg sign); often diagnosed late on CT.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: How are groin hernias repaired?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: Open mesh repair (Lichtenstein) or laparoscopic (TEP / TAPP) for inguinal hernias; femoral hernias are repaired promptly (open or laparoscopic). Strangulated hernias need emergency surgery with assessment of bowel viability.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What are the main complications of hernia repair?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back:
• Recurrence
  • chronic groin pain (ilioinguinal / genitofemoral nerve)
  • haematoma / seroma
  • wound infection
  • and (in men) ischaemic orchitis / testicular atrophy.
Mesh reduces recurrence but can rarely cause chronic pain.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What does a cough impulse tell you, and when is it absent?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A palpable expansile impulse on coughing indicates a hernia (a communication with the abdominal cavity); note a saphena varix also transmits a cough impulse/thrill, via the venous system. It is lost when a hernia becomes incarcerated or strangulated — an important warning sign.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: How do you tell a scrotal swelling from a groin (inguinoscrotal) lump?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: If you can get above the swelling, it is scrotal in origin (e.g. hydrocele, epididymal cyst); if you cannot get above it, it is an inguinoscrotal hernia descending from the groin.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: How does a paediatric inguinal hernia present and how is it managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: Almost always indirect (a patent processus vaginalis) — an intermittent groin / scrotal lump in an infant. They have a high incarceration risk, so are repaired promptly (herniotomy); an incarcerated hernia warrants gentle reduction then semi-urgent repair. In girls the sac may contain an ovary.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What is a Spigelian hernia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A hernia through the Spigelian fascia at the semilunar line (the lateral border of rectus, usually below the arcuate line) — often interparietal / occult with localised pain and a high strangulation risk; diagnosed on ultrasound / CT.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.front: What groin-lump differentials are specific to women?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump.back: A round-ligament varicosity (enlarges in pregnancy, disappears on lying) and a hydrocele of the canal of Nuck (a fluid-filled, transilluminable swelling — the female equivalent of a hydrocele of the cord); femoral hernias are also commoner in women.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is heartburn (pyrosis), and is it a symptom or a diagnosis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Heartburn (pyrosis) is a symptom — a retrosternal burning sensation, worse on lying flat, bending or after meals, often relieved by antacids. It is not a diagnosis; its commonest cause is GORD.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is acid regurgitation, and how does it differ from vomiting?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: The effortless return of acid or food from the stomach to the throat / mouth, without nausea or retching — unlike vomiting, which is forceful and preceded by nausea. It is a cardinal symptom of reflux.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is waterbrash?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: A sudden filling of the mouth with saliva, triggered reflexively by oesophageal acid — a classic accompanying symptom of reflux (distinct from regurgitated acid itself).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is the commonest cause of heartburn and acid regurgitation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) — reflux of gastric contents through an incompetent lower oesophageal sphincter, causing symptoms and/or mucosal damage.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is the underlying mechanism of GORD?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: A weak or transiently-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) allowing acid reflux, often with a hiatus hernia and raised intra-abdominal pressure (obesity, pregnancy) — overwhelming the normal anti-reflux barrier.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: Which lifestyle and dietary factors trigger or worsen reflux?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back:
• Obesity, large / late meals, fatty and spicy food, caffeine, chocolate, alcohol and smoking
  • lying down or bending after meals
  • and tight clothing
— all raise reflux or lower LOS tone.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: Which drugs can worsen reflux by lowering LOS tone?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Nitrates, calcium-channel blockers, anticholinergics, theophylline and beta-agonists relax the LOS; NSAIDs / bisphosphonates can also cause direct mucosal irritation. Review the drug chart.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is a hiatus hernia and how does it relate to reflux?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Herniation of the proximal stomach through the diaphragmatic hiatus into the thorax. A sliding hiatus hernia (commonest) disrupts the anti-reflux barrier and predisposes to GORD; a rolling / para-oesophageal hernia can strangulate.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What are the extra-oesophageal (atypical) manifestations of reflux?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Chronic cough, nocturnal wheeze / asthma, hoarseness and laryngitis, globus sensation, recurrent sore throat / sinusitis, and dental erosion — and non-cardiac chest pain. Reflux irritates the larynx and airway.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Reflux reaching the larynx and pharynx, causing hoarseness, chronic throat-clearing, cough and globus — often without prominent heartburn (‘silent reflux’). ENT may see posterior laryngeal inflammation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: Where do H2-receptor antagonists fit in the treatment of reflux?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: H₂-receptor antagonists (e.g. famotidine — the main one still routinely available in the UK) reduce histamine-driven acid secretion but are weaker than PPIs. They are an add-on for nocturnal breakthrough or an alternative when a PPI is not tolerated. (Ranitidine was withdrawn over NDMA contamination.)

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What are the red-flag features in reflux that mandate endoscopy?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back:
• Dysphagia (any age)
  • weight loss
  • GI bleeding / iron-deficiency anaemia
  • persistent vomiting
  • an epigastric mass
  • and new reflux at age ≥55 with weight loss
— to exclude oesophageal / gastric cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What are the complications of long-standing GORD?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back:
• Reflux oesophagitis
  • peptic stricture (causing dysphagia)
  • Barrett’s oesophagus (with its risk of adenocarcinoma)
  • aspiration
  • chronic anaemia and dental erosion.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is a peptic (reflux) stricture and how does it present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: A fibrotic narrowing of the lower oesophagus from chronic acid injury, presenting with progressive dysphagia to solids. It needs endoscopy (to exclude malignancy) and endoscopic dilatation plus acid suppression.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is Barrett's oesophagus and why does it matter in reflux?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Metaplasia of the lower-oesophageal lining from squamous to columnar epithelium due to chronic reflux — a premalignant change raising the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma; it requires surveillance endoscopy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is the first step in managing typical reflux without red flags?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Lifestyle change (weight loss, smaller / earlier meals, stop smoking, cut alcohol / caffeine, raise the bed head) plus an antacid / alginate or a trial of a full-dose PPI (4–8 weeks).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: How do alginates work in reflux?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: They form a viscous ‘raft’ that floats on the gastric contents, physically blocking reflux and protecting the oesophageal mucosa — useful for symptomatic and postprandial / nocturnal relief.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is the mainstay of medical treatment for GORD?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: A proton pump inhibitor (PPI) (e.g. omeprazole, lansoprazole) — the most effective acid suppression; use a full-dose trial then step down to the lowest effective dose.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is the diagnostic gold-standard investigation for GORD?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: 24-hour ambulatory oesophageal pH (with impedance) monitoring — it quantifies acid (and non-acid) reflux and correlates it with symptoms. It is used when the diagnosis is unclear, symptoms are refractory, or before surgery.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: Why is oesophageal manometry done before anti-reflux surgery?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: To confirm oesophageal peristalsis and exclude a motility disorder such as achalasia (which fundoplication would worsen) — and to position the pH probe. It is a mandatory pre-operative assessment.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is the surgical option for GORD, and when is it considered?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Laparoscopic (Nissen) fundoplication — wrapping the gastric fundus around the lower oesophagus to recreate the anti-reflux barrier. Considered for refractory symptoms, PPI intolerance, or volume reflux in confirmed GORD.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What are the recognised side-effects of fundoplication?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Dysphagia (usually transient), gas-bloat syndrome, inability to belch or vomit, and flatulence — from the tightened wrap. Symptoms often settle but can be troublesome.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: How is reflux in pregnancy managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Reflux is common (progesterone relaxes the LOS; the gravid uterus raises intra-abdominal pressure). Start with lifestyle measures and antacids / alginates; omeprazole is used if needed and is considered safe in pregnancy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: How does the pain of reflux differ from cardiac chest pain?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Reflux: burning, related to meals and posture (worse lying / bending), relieved by antacids. Cardiac: exertional, radiating to arm / jaw, with sweating / breathlessness. Overlap is common — ECG when in doubt.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is globus sensation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: A persistent feeling of a lump in the throat with no true dysphagia — can be associated with reflux (LPR) or anxiety. True, progressive dysphagia is a red flag and must be distinguished from globus.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What causes odynophagia (painful swallowing) rather than simple reflux?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Infective oesophagitis (Candida — in the immunocompromised, or inhaled-steroid users; also HSV / CMV) or pill oesophagitis (e.g. bisphosphonates, doxycycline taken without water). It points away from simple GORD.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: Why can chronic reflux cause dental erosion?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Refluxed gastric acid reaching the mouth demineralises tooth enamel, typically the palatal surfaces of the upper teeth — a clue to occult / nocturnal reflux, often noticed by the dentist.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: How does reflux interact with asthma?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Reflux can trigger or worsen asthma (micro-aspiration and vagally-mediated bronchoconstriction), and some asthma drugs (beta-agonists, theophylline) worsen reflux — consider reflux in poorly-controlled nocturnal asthma.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: When is empirical PPI treatment appropriate rather than immediate endoscopy?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: In typical reflux with no red flags and age <55 — a lifestyle + PPI trial is first-line. Endoscopy is reserved for red flags, refractory symptoms, or diagnostic uncertainty.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: Why should a PPI be stopped before oesophageal pH studies (and H. pylori testing)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: A PPI suppresses acid and the organism, giving false-negative results. Stop the PPI (typically for ~1 week before pH studies, and 2 weeks before H. pylori testing) so the test reflects the true state.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What advice reduces nocturnal reflux specifically?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Avoid eating within ~3 hours of lying down, raise the head of the bed (e.g. blocks under the bedposts), and lose weight — gravity and an empty stomach reduce night-time reflux.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What is the significance of new dysphagia developing in a patient with long-standing reflux?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: It is a red flag — it may indicate a benign peptic stricture or an oesophageal adenocarcinoma (often on a background of Barrett’s). It mandates urgent endoscopy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: Why is chronic reflux linked specifically to oesophageal ADENOcarcinoma?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back: Chronic acid reflux drives Barrett’s metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma in the lower oesophagus. (Squamous-cell oesophageal cancer, by contrast, is linked to smoking / alcohol and the upper two-thirds.)

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.front: What are the harms of long-term PPI use, and the prescribing principle?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Aci.back:
• Hypomagnesaemia
  • low vitamin B12
  • increased C. difficile / enteric infection
  • fracture / osteoporosis risk
  • and rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping.
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and review / step down once symptoms are controlled.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: How do you distinguish an enlarged spleen from an enlarged liver on examination?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Both are dull, move with respiration and you cannot get above them. The spleen (LUQ) has a notch, enlarges towards the RIF and is not ballotable; the liver (RUQ) enlarges below the right costal margin. Palpate from the RIF upwards on inspiration.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: How do you distinguish splenomegaly from an enlarged left kidney?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: The kidney is ballotable (bimanually palpable), you can get above it, has no notch, and there is a band of resonant bowel over it. The spleen is dull, notched, not ballotable and you cannot get above it.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: Where should you begin palpating for hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, and why?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: In the right iliac fossa, moving up towards each costal margin as the patient breathes in — a massively enlarged organ can extend into the RIF and be missed if you start too high.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What features of a palpable liver suggest malignancy?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: A hard, craggy, irregular (nodular) liver edge, often with weight loss — suggesting metastases (the commonest cause of a craggy liver) or hepatocellular carcinoma. A smooth liver is more suggestive of a benign / congestive cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What are the main causes of hepatomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back:
• Cirrhosis (early), alcohol and NAFLD
  • malignancy (metastases, HCC)
  • congestion (right heart failure, Budd-Chiari)
  • infection (viral hepatitis, abscess)
  • and infiltration (amyloid, haemochromatosis, myeloproliferative disease).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What are the features of hepatomegaly from right heart failure (congestion)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: A smooth, tender, often pulsatile liver (pulsatile with tricuspid regurgitation), with a raised JVP and peripheral oedema. The liver may shrink after diuresis; look for the underlying cardiac cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What are the main categories of splenomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back:
• Portal hypertension (cirrhosis)
  • haematological (leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloproliferative disease)
  • infective (EBV / glandular fever, malaria, infective endocarditis, TB)
  • haemolytic anaemias
  • and infiltration (amyloid, Gaucher’s).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What are the causes of MASSIVE splenomegaly (spleen crossing the midline / reaching the RIF)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Chronic myeloid leukaemia, myelofibrosis, and malaria / visceral leishmaniasis (and, in endemic areas, tropical splenomegaly) — a much shorter list than the many causes of mild–moderate splenomegaly.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What are the causes of hepatosplenomegaly (both organs enlarged)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back:
• Chronic liver disease with portal hypertension
  • haematological malignancy (lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloproliferative disorders)
  • infection (EBV, malaria, viral hepatitis)
  • and infiltration / storage (amyloid, sarcoid, Gaucher’s).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: Why should patients with splenomegaly avoid contact sports?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Because an enlarged spleen is at risk of rupture (e.g. after minor trauma), which can cause life-threatening haemorrhage — a classic warning in glandular fever (EBV), where sport is avoided for several weeks.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What is the first-line imaging to confirm hepatomegaly or splenomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Ultrasound — it confirms organ size, characterises the texture / focal lesions, and assesses the portal vein and any ascites; CT is used to characterise and stage further.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: Which blood tests start the work-up of organomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back:
• FBC and a blood film (cytopenias, blasts, malaria parasites, abnormal cells)
  • LFTs and clotting
  • viral serology
  • ferritin / iron studies
  • LDH
  • and an autoimmune screen
— guided by the pattern.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: How does portal hypertension cause splenomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Raised portal venous pressure (usually from cirrhosis) causes congestive splenomegaly — often with other features of portal hypertension (ascites, caput medusae, varices) and hypersplenism (thrombocytopenia).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What is hypersplenism?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Overactive splenic sequestration and destruction of blood cells in an enlarged spleen — causing cytopenias (especially thrombocytopenia, also anaemia / leucopenia) with a cellular marrow; it can accompany splenomegaly of any cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: Which infections classically cause splenomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back:
• EBV (glandular fever)
  • malaria and visceral leishmaniasis (massive)
  • infective endocarditis
  • TB
  • and viral hepatitis
— take a travel and exposure history.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What haematological malignancies cause splenomegaly, and how do they present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Chronic myeloid leukaemia and myelofibrosis (often massive), lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukaemia — with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), lymphadenopathy and abnormal blood counts; confirm with a film, marrow and node biopsy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What is the commonest cause of a hard, craggy, nodular liver?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Liver metastases — the liver is a very common site for spread (e.g. colorectal, breast, lung, pancreatic). Primary hepatocellular carcinoma (usually on a background of cirrhosis) is the other key malignant cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What examination findings suggest that organomegaly is due to chronic liver disease?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, leukonychia, gynaecomastia, caput medusae), jaundice, ascites and asterixis — pointing to cirrhosis with portal hypertension.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: How is a hepatic or splenic cause confirmed once the organ is identified?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Ultrasound first, then targeted tests: CT and biopsy for a hepatic mass; blood film and bone marrow ± lymph-node biopsy for a haematological cause; thick & thin films for malaria; fibroscan for cirrhosis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What non-organ swellings can mimic hepatomegaly or splenomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: A Riedel’s lobe (a normal liver variant), an enlarged kidney (ballotable, resonant band over it), and other masses / lymph nodes — the exam discriminators separate them.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What is Budd-Chiari syndrome and how does it relate to hepatomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Hepatic venous outflow obstruction (hepatic-vein / IVC thrombosis) — presenting with tender hepatomegaly, ascites and abdominal pain; associated with prothrombotic states. Diagnosed on Doppler ultrasound.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: Why is a blood film central to the assessment of splenomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back:
It can reveal the cause directly —
  • blasts (acute leukaemia)
  • a left shift / basophilia (CML)
  • lymphocytosis (CLL / lymphoma)
  • malaria parasites
  • spherocytes (haemolysis) or teardrop cells (myelofibrosis)
— and shows any hypersplenic cytopenias.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: How is the spleen's size described / graded clinically?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: By how far it extends below the left costal margin (in cm or finger-breadths) towards the umbilicus / RIF; a spleen must usually be ~3× enlarged before it is palpable, so a palpable spleen is always abnormal.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: How can you detect splenomegaly by percussion before it is palpable?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Percuss Traube’s space (the lower-left anterior chest over the gastric air bubble) — dullness suggests splenic enlargement; Castell’s sign is dullness in the lowest left intercostal space on full inspiration. Both detect early splenomegaly before it is palpable.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What features distinguish infective (e.g. EBV) from malignant causes of hepatosplenomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Infective: often acute, with fever, sore throat / lymphadenopathy and a self-limiting course (EBV), or travel exposure (malaria). Malignant: more insidious, with B symptoms, weight loss, persistent lymphadenopathy and abnormal counts — needing a film, marrow and biopsy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: Which infiltrative / storage disorders cause organomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back:
• Amyloidosis and sarcoidosis (hepatosplenomegaly)
  • haemochromatosis (iron — hepatomegaly)
  • and storage diseases such as Gaucher’s (massive splenomegaly)
— suggested when common causes are excluded.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What is the significance of splenomegaly with lymphadenopathy?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: It strongly suggests a lymphoproliferative disorder (lymphoma or CLL) or an infection (EBV, HIV, TB) — examine all node groups, check a blood film, and arrange lymph-node biopsy if malignancy is suspected.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: How does the direction of enlargement help identify the spleen?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: The spleen enlarges diagonally towards the right iliac fossa (down and medially) — so you palpate for its edge coming from the LUQ towards the RIF, and it has a notch on its medial border.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: When is splenectomy considered, and what is a key consequence?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: For trauma / rupture, refractory hypersplenism / haematological disease, or a massive symptomatic spleen. Afterwards the patient is at risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection from encapsulated organisms (and reactive thrombocytosis / VTE) — needing vaccination and lifelong prophylactic penicillin.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What is Felty's syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: The triad of rheumatoid arthritis + splenomegaly + neutropenia — a classic association to recognise in a patient with long-standing RA and a palpable spleen; the neutropenia predisposes to infection.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: How can splenomegaly or portal hypertension occur without cirrhosis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: Portal vein thrombosis causes pre-hepatic portal hypertension (splenomegaly and varices with a normal liver); splenic vein thrombosis (often from pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer) causes isolated splenomegaly and gastric varices.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What are the causes of massive hepatomegaly?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back:
• Metastases
  • myeloproliferative disease / myelofibrosis
  • alcoholic fatty liver
  • hepatocellular carcinoma
  • and infiltration (amyloid)
— the parallel shortlist to massive splenomegaly.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.front: What is the significance of a hepatic bruit or a friction rub over the liver?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Hepatomegaly &.back: A hepatic bruit suggests hepatocellular carcinoma or alcoholic hepatitis (increased vascularity); a friction rub suggests a tumour, infarct or perihepatitis — both are auscultatory clues over an enlarged liver.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What is jaundice and at what level does it become clinically visible?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Yellow discolouration of the sclera and skin from a raised serum bilirubin — usually clinically visible once bilirubin exceeds ~50 µmol/L (roughly 3× the upper limit; best seen in the sclera / under the tongue).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What are the three categories of jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back:
• Pre-hepatic (unconjugated — haemolysis, Gilbert’s)
  • hepatic / hepatocellular (hepatitis, alcohol, drugs, cirrhosis)
  • and post-hepatic (conjugated / obstructive — stones, tumour, PBC / PSC).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: How do urine and stool colour help localise jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Dark urine means conjugated bilirubin (hepatocellular or obstructive); pale stool + itch points specifically to obstruction. Normal-coloured urine and stool suggests a pre-hepatic (unconjugated) cause. So urine/stool separates pre-hepatic from the rest, not obstruction from everything.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: Why does unconjugated bilirubin not appear in the urine?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble and bound to albumin, so it cannot be filtered by the kidney — hence ‘acholuric’ jaundice (normal-coloured urine) in haemolysis and Gilbert’s. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and does appear in urine.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: How does the LFT pattern distinguish hepatocellular from cholestatic jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: A hepatocellular picture shows a predominant rise in ALT / AST (transaminases); a cholestatic / obstructive picture shows a predominant rise in ALP and GGT. A raised GGT confirms the ALP is of hepatic origin.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What is Gilbert's syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: A common, benign inherited defect of bilirubin conjugation (reduced UGT1A1) causing a mild isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, typically on fasting, illness or stress, with otherwise normal LFTs and no haemolysis. It needs no treatment.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What blood tests confirm haemolysis as a cause of jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Raised unconjugated bilirubin, raised LDH, raised reticulocytes and low haptoglobin, with anaemia and a suggestive blood film; a direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test identifies immune haemolysis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What is Charcot's triad and what does it indicate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Fever (with rigors), right-upper-quadrant pain and jaundice — the triad of ascending cholangitis (infection of an obstructed biliary tree). Add confusion and hypotension and it becomes Reynolds’ pentad.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: How is ascending cholangitis managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: As a biliary-sepsis emergency: resuscitation and the sepsis six, IV antibiotics, and urgent biliary drainage — usually ERCP (or percutaneous / surgical drainage if ERCP fails).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What is Courvoisier's law and what does it imply?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: In painless jaundice, a palpable (distended) gallbladder is unlikely to be gallstones — it suggests malignant obstruction (pancreatic head cancer or cholangiocarcinoma). Stones cause a fibrotic, non-distensible gallbladder.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What are the features of acute liver failure?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Jaundice with hepatic encephalopathy and coagulopathy (raised INR) developing in someone without pre-existing chronic liver disease — often from paracetamol overdose, viral hepatitis or drugs. It needs urgent specialist / transplant-centre care.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: Why is a raised INR / prothrombin time important in jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: The liver makes clotting factors, so a rising INR / prolonged PT reflects failing synthetic function — a marker of severity in acute liver failure and a key prognostic variable (e.g. in the King’s College criteria).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What are the common causes of hepatocellular jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back:
• Viral hepatitis (A–E)
  • alcoholic hepatitis
  • drug-induced liver injury (paracetamol)
  • autoimmune hepatitis
  • cirrhosis of any cause and hepatocellular carcinoma
— all give a predominantly transaminase (ALT / AST) rise.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What distinguishes alcoholic hepatitis biochemically?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: An AST:ALT ratio >2:1 (often with a raised GGT and macrocytosis) in the context of an alcohol history — unlike viral hepatitis, where ALT usually predominates.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What are the common causes of obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Common bile duct stones, pancreatic head cancer and cholangiocarcinoma; also primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, strictures and (rarely) pancreatitis / nodes compressing the duct.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What are the features of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: A middle-aged woman with fatigue, pruritus and cholestatic LFTs (↑ALP), positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA) and a raised IgM. Treated with ursodeoxycholic acid.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What are the features of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Progressive cholestasis (↑ALP) in a patient often with ulcerative colitis; MRCP shows multifocal strictures and a ‘beaded’ biliary tree. It raises the risk of cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What is the first-line imaging in jaundice, and what is the key finding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Ultrasound — the key question is whether the bile ducts are dilated: dilated = obstruction (post-hepatic; proceed to MRCP / CT / ERCP); non-dilated favours a hepatocellular or pre-hepatic cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What is the role of MRCP versus ERCP in obstructive jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: MRCP is a non-invasive scan to map the biliary tree and find the level / cause of obstruction; ERCP is therapeutic (stone extraction, stenting, brushings) and is reserved for intervention because it carries a risk of pancreatitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: Which initial blood tests should be sent in a jaundiced patient?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back:
• LFTs with a split (conjugated / unconjugated) bilirubin
  • FBC, blood film, reticulocytes, LDH, haptoglobin (haemolysis)
  • clotting / albumin (synthetic function)
  • viral hepatitis serology and autoantibodies (AMA, ASMA).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What causes pruritus in cholestatic jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Retained bile salts / cholephiles in cholestasis cause itch (often severe, worse at night). It is a marker of a conjugated / obstructive picture; treatments include colestyramine and treating the obstruction.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: How does neonatal jaundice differ in its significance by timing?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back:
• First 24 hours: always pathological (haemolysis — rhesus / ABO, sepsis)
  • days 2–14: usually physiological (or early breastfeeding / dehydration jaundice), unconjugated
  • >14 days (prolonged) needs a split bilirubin — unconjugated causes include benign breast-milk jaundice and hypothyroidism, while a conjugated rise means biliary atresia until excluded.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What is the significance of conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia in a neonate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: It is never physiological — pale stools and dark urine with conjugated jaundice suggest biliary atresia, which needs urgent diagnosis and surgery (Kasai portoenterostomy) before ~8 weeks; other causes include neonatal hepatitis and metabolic disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: Why must paracetamol levels be checked in acute jaundice / liver failure?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Paracetamol overdose is a leading cause of acute liver failure and is treatable with N-acetylcysteine; levels (with a timed history) guide treatment on the nomogram, and NAC is given empirically in staggered / late or fulminant presentations.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What is the difference between conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin metabolism?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Unconjugated bilirubin (from haem breakdown) is fat-soluble, albumin-bound and taken to the liver; the liver conjugates it (water-soluble) and excretes it in bile. Gut bacteria convert it to stercobilin (stool) and urobilinogen (some reabsorbed → urine).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: How does urinary urobilinogen change in haemolysis versus obstruction?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Haemolysis: increased bilirubin load → raised urinary urobilinogen (urine may darken on standing). Complete obstruction: no bilirubin reaches the gut → absent urinary urobilinogen with dark urine (from conjugated bilirubin) and pale stools.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What examination findings suggest chronic liver disease as the cause of jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back:
Peripheral stigmata:
  • spider naevi
  • palmar erythema
  • leukonychia
  • gynaecomastia
  • Dupuytren’s
  • caput medusae
  • ascites
  • splenomegaly and asterixis (encephalopathy)
— pointing to cirrhosis rather than an acute or obstructive cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What tumour markers may help in obstructive jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: CA19-9 (pancreatic / cholangiocarcinoma) and AFP (hepatocellular carcinoma) — they support a diagnosis alongside imaging but do not replace tissue; CA19-9 can be falsely raised by cholestasis itself.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What is the classic presentation of pancreatic head cancer?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Painless, progressive obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stools, itch) with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier) — investigate with CT and CA19-9; often presents late.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: Which drugs commonly cause a cholestatic or hepatocellular drug-induced jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back:
• Cholestatic: co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin, chlorpromazine, anabolic steroids, the OCP.
  • Hepatocellular: paracetamol (overdose), isoniazid, statins, methotrexate, anti-epileptics
— take a careful drug history.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: Which inherited liver diseases cause hepatocellular jaundice in a young patient?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Wilson’s disease (copper — Kayser-Fleischer rings, neuropsychiatric signs, low caeruloplasmin; can present as acute liver failure with Coombs-negative haemolysis and a low ALP) and hereditary haemochromatosis (iron overload). Also α1-antitrypsin deficiency and autoimmune hepatitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What are the consequences of chronic cholestasis besides jaundice?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Pruritus, and malabsorption of fat (steatorrhoea) and the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. Vitamin K deficiency causes a coagulopathy that corrects with parenteral vitamin K — distinguishing it from the coagulopathy of hepatic synthetic failure (which does not).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What organisms cause ascending cholangitis and what cultures should be taken?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Usually gut organisms — E. coli, Klebsiella and Enterococcus. Send blood cultures before antibiotics; severity / diagnosis can be graded with the Tokyo Guidelines. Definitive treatment is biliary drainage (ERCP).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: How is significant neonatal (unconjugated) jaundice treated?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Phototherapy (converts bilirubin to a water-soluble form) guided by age-specific treatment thresholds (Bhutani / NICE charts); exchange transfusion for very high or rapidly rising levels — to prevent kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy / basal-ganglia deposition).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What are the inherited conjugated hyperbilirubinaemias?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Dubin-Johnson syndrome (defective canalicular excretion — a benign conjugated rise with a characteristic black liver) and Rotor syndrome (similar, benign, non-pigmented) — the conjugated counterparts to Gilbert’s; both benign and need no treatment.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.front: What is Mirizzi syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice.back: Obstructive jaundice from a gallstone impacted in the cystic duct / Hartmann’s pouch compressing the common hepatic duct — a gallstone cause of obstruction without a stone in the CBD itself; diagnosed on MRCP.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.back: Whitening of the nails. It is divided into true leukonychia (the nail plate is white) and apparent leukonychia (the nail bed is pale, seen through a clear plate).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.front: How do you distinguish true from apparent leukonychia at the bedside?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.back: Apply pressure / blanch the nail: apparent leukonychia blanches (it is nail-bed vascular change) and does not move with growth; true leukonychia does not blanch and moves distally as the nail grows.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.front: What does diffuse true leukonychia (leukonychia totalis) indicate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.back: Hypoalbuminaemia — a low serum albumin from any cause (chronic liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy, malnutrition); it can also be hereditary. It is a marker of low albumin, not liver-specific.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.front: What are the causes of the hypoalbuminaemia behind leukonychia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.back:
• Reduced synthesis (chronic liver disease / cirrhosis)
  • urinary loss (nephrotic syndrome)
  • gut loss (protein-losing enteropathy — IBD, coeliac)
  • poor intake (malnutrition)
  • and severe illness / sepsis (capillary leak + negative acute phase).
A nail showing a proximal white ‘ground-glass’ appearance with a normal 1–2 mm distal band (an apparent leukonychia) — associated with cirrhosis, chronic heart failure and diabetes.
Paired transverse white lines across the nail that do not move with nail growth (they are in the nail bed) — a sign of hypoalbuminaemia; they resolve when albumin normalises.
A nail with the proximal half white and the distal half red-brown / pink — classically a sign of chronic kidney disease.
Transverse white bands in the nail plate that grow out distally (true leukonychia) — caused by arsenic / thallium (heavy-metal) poisoning, chemotherapy, or severe systemic illness.
Small white spots in the nail plate — extremely common and benign, usually from minor trauma to the nail matrix. It is not a reliable sign of calcium or zinc deficiency (a common myth).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.front: How does a fungal white nail (superficial white onychomycosis) differ from true/apparent leukonychia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.back: Pseudoleukonychia from fungal infection gives a chalky-white, crumbly nail, often with onycholysis or dystrophy, and is confirmed on nail clippings for microscopy & culture — unlike true (plate) or apparent (bed) leukonychia, where the nail is otherwise smooth and intact.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.front: How do Beau's lines differ from the white transverse lines of leukonychia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.back: Beau’s lines are transverse grooves / ridges (not white) from temporary nail-matrix arrest in severe systemic illness; the transverse lines of Muehrcke’s and Mees’ are a colour change without a groove.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.front: Which other stigmata should you look for when leukonychia is seen in suspected liver disease?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.back:
The other chronic-liver-disease stigmata:
  • spider naevi
  • palmar erythema
  • gynaecomastia
  • Dupuytren’s
  • jaundice
  • ascites
  • and asterixis
— but also screen for renal and gut causes of low albumin.
By causing hypoalbuminaemia through heavy urinary protein loss (>3.5 g/day) — with oedema and hyperlipidaemia; the low albumin produces the white nails (Muehrcke’s lines / leukonychia).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.front: What is protein-losing enteropathy as a cause of leukonychia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.back:
Excessive loss of protein (albumin) through the gut mucosa — in
  • IBD
  • coeliac disease
  • lymphangiectasia
  • and severe gastroenteritis
— producing hypoalbuminaemia and its nail signs.

It is not treated in itself — management is directed at the underlying cause (correct the hypoalbuminaemia / treat the liver, renal or gut disease). Punctata and hereditary leukonychia need only reassurance.
Serum albumin first; then LFTs (liver), urinalysis and urine protein:creatinine (nephrotic), coeliac serology, U&E (CKD / half-and-half nails) and a nutritional assessment.
A change in the nail bed / its vasculature (e.g. oedema of the bed or altered vascularity) seen through a translucent, normal nail plate — hence it blanches and does not move with growth.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.front: Do isolated white spots or streaks on the nails need investigation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Leukonychia.back: No — leukonychia punctata (spots) and longitudinal striate leukonychia are common normal variants from minor trauma (not calcium or zinc deficiency, a popular myth); isolated white spots in a well patient need no blood tests. Only diffuse true leukonychia warrants checking albumin.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: Migratory (recurrent) superficial thrombophlebitis — tender, red, cord-like inflamed superficial veins that appear in successive, changing sites — as a paraneoplastic marker of an occult malignancy.
It resolves and reappears in different sites over time, often in unusual locations (arms, chest, trunk) rather than a single varicose leg vein — this migrating, multi-site pattern is the key feature.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: Which malignancy is classically associated with Trousseau's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma — the strongest and classic association; also lung, gastric, colorectal and ovarian adenocarcinomas.
