signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: Besides pancreatic cancer, which cancers cause migratory thrombophlebitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: Other adenocarcinomas: lung, gastric, colorectal and ovarian — and other mucin-secreting tumours.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: What is the mechanism of Trousseau's sign of malignancy?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: A cancer-associated hypercoagulable state — tumours release tissue factor and mucins that activate the clotting cascade, causing recurrent superficial (and deep) venous thromboses.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: There are two 'Trousseau's signs' — what are they?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: Trousseau’s sign of malignancy (migratory thrombophlebitis → occult cancer) and Trousseau’s sign of latent tetany (carpal spasm on inflating a BP cuff → hypocalcaemia) — same name, different signs.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: How does migratory thrombophlebitis differ from ordinary superficial thrombophlebitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: Ordinary superficial thrombophlebitis is usually a single site over a varicose vein or cannula and is benign. Trousseau’s is recurrent, migratory and multi-site, flagging an occult cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: How is Trousseau's sign related to DVT and PE?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: It is part of the spectrum of cancer-associated thrombosis — the same hypercoagulable state also causes DVT and PE, which should be actively excluded.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: What investigations are appropriate when Trousseau's sign is found?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back:
Investigate for an occult cancer:
  • bloods
  • CT chest / abdomen / pelvis
  • age-appropriate cancer screen
  • tumour markers (e.g. CA 19-9)
  • and Doppler ultrasound if DVT is suspected.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: What is the preferred anticoagulant for cancer-associated thrombosis in Trousseau's syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is preferred; warfarin is relatively ineffective in this setting. DOACs are also used in many cancer-associated VTE cases, but are relatively avoided in luminal GI / genitourinary cancers (bleeding risk), where LMWH remains preferred.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: Why is warfarin relatively ineffective in Trousseau's syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: The strong tumour-driven procoagulant activity (tissue factor / mucins) tends to break through warfarin anticoagulation, so LMWH (or a DOAC) gives better control.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: What does a segment of superficial thrombophlebitis feel like on examination?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: A tender, firm, cord-like palpable superficial vein with overlying erythema and warmth — localised to the affected vein.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: What other paraneoplastic thrombotic complication shares the same hypercoagulable mechanism?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: Non-bacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis — sterile fibrin-platelet valve vegetations in mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas that can embolise (e.g. stroke). It is part of the same cancer-associated hypercoagulable spectrum as Trousseau’s sign.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: Why is the eponym attached to Armand Trousseau?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: Armand Trousseau described the association of migratory thrombophlebitis with malignancy — and later recognised the sign in himself, subsequently found to have (gastric) cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: What should recurrent unprovoked VTE prompt you to consider?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: An occult malignancy — recurrent or unprovoked venous thromboembolism (like migratory thrombophlebitis) can be a paraneoplastic marker warranting cancer assessment.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: Which tumour marker is useful when pancreatic cancer is suspected as the cause?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: CA 19-9 — associated with pancreatic and biliary malignancy (supportive, not a screening test); CA 125 is the analogous marker if ovarian cancer is suspected.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: What imaging best searches for the occult primary in Trousseau's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis (CT CAP) — to look for a pancreatic, lung, GI or ovarian primary; further targeted imaging / endoscopy follows the findings.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.front: What does 'paraneoplastic' mean in the context of Trousseau's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Migratory Throm.back: A remote effect of a cancer not due to local tumour invasion or metastasis — here, tumour-driven hypercoagulability causing migratory thrombophlebitis, which may precede the cancer diagnosis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: Place your fingers at the right upper quadrant (costal margin, mid-clavicular line, over the gallbladder fundus) and ask the patient to breathe in deeply. Watch for an arrest of inspiration caused by pain.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: What are the classic risk factors for gallstones?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back:
The 5 Fs:
  • Fat
  • Female
  • Forty (40+)
  • Fertile (multiparous)
  • and Family history.
Gallstones underlie the whole biliary spectrum — biliary colic, cholecystitis, CBD stones and gallstone pancreatitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: Why must Murphy's sign be negative on the left side to count as positive?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: To confirm the response is specific to the gallbladder (RUQ) rather than generalised abdominal tenderness. A true positive is present on the right and absent on the left.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: What condition does a positive Murphy's sign indicate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: Acute cholecystitis — inflammation of the gallbladder wall, usually from a stone impacted in the cystic duct, obstructing gallbladder outflow.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: What is Charcot's triad and what does it indicate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: RUQ pain + fever / rigors + jaundice — it indicates ascending cholangitis (infection of an obstructed biliary tree), an emergency needing resuscitation, IV antibiotics and biliary decompression (ERCP).
Charcot’s triad (RUQ pain + fever + jaundice) PLUS hypotension and confusion — indicating septic shock from severe ascending cholangitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: How do biliary colic and acute cholecystitis differ clinically?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: Biliary colic: RUQ / epigastric pain after fatty food, lasts <6 hours, no fever, normal inflammatory markers, Murphy’s usually negative — managed with analgesia and elective (planned) laparoscopic cholecystectomy; antibiotics are NOT indicated (no infection). Acute cholecystitis: constant pain >6 hours, fever, positive Murphy’s, raised WCC / CRP — needs antibiotics.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: What is the usual underlying cause of acute cholecystitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: A gallstone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann’s pouch, obstructing gallbladder outflow and causing wall inflammation (± secondary infection). A minority is acalculous.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: What LFT pattern is expected in uncomplicated acute cholecystitis, and what does derangement suggest?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: LFTs are usually near-normal in cholecystitis. Marked derangement / jaundice suggests a common bile duct stone or Mirizzi syndrome (a stone in the cystic duct / Hartmann’s pouch compressing the common hepatic duct).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: What is choledocholithiasis and how does it present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: A stone in the common bile duct — causing obstructive jaundice, a dilated CBD and deranged (obstructive) LFTs; it risks ascending cholangitis and gallstone pancreatitis.
Epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised amylase / lipase, when a gallstone obstructs the ampulla; it is a key complication of gallstone disease to exclude in biliary pain.

Maximal tenderness directly over the gallbladder when it is compressed by the ultrasound probe. Combined with a thick-walled, stone-filled gallbladder and pericholecystic fluid, it is highly suggestive of acute cholecystitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: What is the first-line imaging investigation for suspected acute cholecystitis, and what does it show?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: Abdominal ultrasound — showing gallstones, a thickened gallbladder wall (>3 mm), pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy’s sign. MRCP is used to look for CBD stones.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: How sensitive and specific is Murphy's sign, and in whom is it unreliable?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: It is relatively specific but only moderately sensitive for acute cholecystitis, and is notably less reliable (blunted) in elderly patients — a negative sign does not exclude the diagnosis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: Name some mimics that can produce RUQ tenderness / a false-positive Murphy's sign.
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back:
• Acute hepatitis (tender liver, deranged LFTs)
  • right lower-lobe pneumonia / pleurisy
  • Fitz-Hugh–Curtis perihepatitis (PID)
  • and a retrocaecal appendix.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: What are the important complications of acute cholecystitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back:
• Empyema of the gallbladder
  • gangrene and perforation (with biliary peritonitis)
  • Mirizzi syndrome
  • and progression to ascending cholangitis or gallstone pancreatitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: What is acalculous cholecystitis and in whom does it occur?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: Acute cholecystitis without gallstones, occurring in the critically ill (sepsis, major surgery / trauma, burns, TPN, ITU patients). It is easily missed, signs are blunted, and it carries a high complication rate.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.front: What is the definitive management of acute (calculous) cholecystitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Murphy's Sign.back: IV fluids, analgesia and antibiotics, then laparoscopic cholecystectomy — ideally early (within about 1 week) of presentation. CBD stones are cleared by ERCP.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What is the difference between vomiting, regurgitation and retching?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
• Vomiting is the forceful ejection of gastric contents (with nausea and retching)
  • Regurgitation is the effortless return of contents without nausea (think GORD / achalasia)
  • Retching is the ‘dry heaves’ — the muscular effort without expulsion.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What are the four sources of input to the medullary vomiting centre?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
• The chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ / area postrema) — drugs, metabolic, toxins
  • vagal / GI afferents — obstruction, irritation
  • the vestibular system — motion, labyrinthitis
  • and higher cortical centres — pain, smell, sight, raised ICP.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Why is the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) able to sense blood-borne emetogens?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: The CTZ (area postrema) lies outside the blood-brain barrier, so it directly samples drugs, toxins and metabolic derangements in the blood and CSF — which is why it mediates drug-, uraemia- and DKA-related vomiting.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What does BILIOUS (green) vomiting indicate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Bile in the vomit means the obstruction / pathology is below the ampulla of Vater (where bile enters, in the second part of the duodenum) — classically small-bowel obstruction. Non-bilious vomiting places the lesion at or above the ampulla (pylorus / proximal duodenum, e.g. pyloric stenosis).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What does FAECULENT vomiting indicate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Distal (large-bowel) or long-standing obstruction, or a gastrocolic fistula — stagnant bowel contents are colonised by bacteria, giving a faecal smell. It is an ominous sign of established obstruction.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What does vomiting UNDIGESTED food hours after eating suggest?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis from chronic PUD, or gastric cancer) or gastroparesis — retained gastric food, often with a succussion splash. Achalasia gives a similar picture but is an oesophageal motility disorder (regurgitation of food retained in the oesophagus).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Which vomit timing patterns are clinically useful clues?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
• Morning vomiting → pregnancy, raised ICP, alcohol / uraemia
  • post-prandial → gastric outlet obstruction / gastroparesis
  • projectile → pyloric stenosis (infant) or raised ICP.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What are the key CENTRAL (non-GI) causes of vomiting?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
• Drugs / toxins (opioids, chemotherapy, digoxin, antibiotics, alcohol)
  • metabolic (DKA, uraemia, hypercalcaemia, hyponatraemia, Addisonian crisis)
  • CNS (raised ICP, migraine)
  • vestibular disease
  • and pregnancy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What are the key PERIPHERAL (GI) causes of vomiting?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
• Gastroenteritis (commonest)
  • bowel obstruction
  • gastric outlet obstruction / gastroparesis
  • peptic ulcer / gastritis
  • pancreatitis
  • biliary disease / cholangitis
  • appendicitis / peritonitis
  • and hepatitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Why must vomiting with a morning headache and focal neurology raise alarm?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: It suggests raised intracranial pressure (tumour, bleed, hydrocephalus). Look for projectile vomiting, papilloedema, early-morning headache worse on coughing / lying flat and focal signs — image the brain (CT head).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What is the classic presentation of infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: A 3–6-week-old (often first-born male) with projectile non-bilious vomiting, who remains hungry; an olive-shaped epigastric mass and visible peristalsis. It causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What electrolyte / acid-base disturbance does prolonged vomiting classically cause?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: A hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis — loss of gastric H⁺ and Cl⁻ raises bicarbonate, and renal K⁺/H⁺ handling worsens the hypokalaemia. Dehydration and pre-renal AKI often accompany it.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What is a Mallory-Weiss tear?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: A mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction caused by forceful retching / vomiting, presenting with haematemesis after an initial bout of non-bloody vomiting. It is usually self-limiting.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What is Boerhaave's syndrome and why is it dangerous?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Full-thickness (transmural) rupture of the oesophagus from forceful vomiting — presenting with severe chest / epigastric pain, subcutaneous (surgical) emphysema and shock. It is life-threatening and needs urgent surgery.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What is a succussion splash and what does it indicate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: A splashing sound heard by shaking the patient’s abdomen (or with a stethoscope) >3 hours after eating — it indicates retained gastric fluid, i.e. gastric outlet obstruction or gastroparesis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Which systemic emergencies can present primarily with vomiting?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
• Inferior MI
  • diabetic ketoacidosis
  • raised ICP
  • Addisonian crisis
  • sepsis
  • and hypercalcaemia
— check an ECG, glucose & ketones, U&E and calcium in unexplained vomiting.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Why can an inferior MI present with nausea and vomiting?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Inferior myocardial ischaemia causes vagal stimulation and shares visceral afferents with the upper gut, producing nausea, vomiting and epigastric discomfort — always ECG a patient with unexplained vomiting and risk factors.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What is the first-line investigation you must not omit in any woman of reproductive age who is vomiting?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: A pregnancy test (βhCG) — to identify pregnancy / hyperemesis gravidarum (and to exclude an ectopic). It changes both the diagnosis and safe prescribing.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What is hyperemesis gravidarum and how is it recognised?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
Severe, protracted vomiting of pregnancy (usually first trimester) causing
  • >5% weight loss
  • dehydration
  • ketosis
  • and electrolyte disturbance
— more severe than ordinary morning sickness and needing admission, fluids and antiemetics.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: How should antiemetics be chosen?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
By mechanism / receptor:
  • cyclizine (H₁ — vestibular, mechanical)
  • ondansetron (5-HT₃ — chemo, post-op)
  • metoclopramide / domperidone (prokinetic D₂ — gastroparesis)
  • haloperidol / prochlorperazine (D₂ — metabolic / drug-induced).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Why should prokinetic antiemetics (metoclopramide/domperidone) be avoided in bowel obstruction?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: They increase gut motility / contraction against the obstruction, worsening pain and risking perforation. In obstruction use an NG tube to decompress and a non-prokinetic antiemetic such as cyclizine or ondansetron.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Why is metoclopramide used with caution, especially in the young?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: It crosses the blood-brain barrier and can cause extrapyramidal side-effects / acute dystonic reactions (especially in young women and children) and, long-term, tardive dyskinesia. Domperidone (which crosses less) is an alternative.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What is the first management priority in a vomiting, dehydrated patient?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Fluid resuscitation and electrolyte correction (especially potassium and chloride) — alongside treating the cause. Antiemetics are adjuncts; they do not correct the fluid and electrolyte deficits.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: How does gastroparesis cause vomiting, and who is at risk?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Delayed gastric emptying from impaired gastric motility causes early satiety, bloating, nausea and vomiting of retained food. It is classically seen in long-standing diabetes (autonomic neuropathy) and after some surgery / drugs.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What features distinguish a vestibular cause of vomiting?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Vertigo (a spinning sensation), nystagmus, and symptoms worse on head movement — e.g. labyrinthitis, BPPV or Ménière’s. Cyclizine (an antihistamine) is the antiemetic of choice.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Which drugs commonly cause nausea and vomiting?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
• Opioids
  • chemotherapy
  • digoxin (toxicity)
  • antibiotics (e.g. macrolides / metronidazole)
  • NSAIDs
  • and SSRIs
— and alcohol. Always review the drug chart in new vomiting.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: How does vomiting cause a pre-renal acute kidney injury?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Loss of fluid causes hypovolaemia and reduced renal perfusion — a pre-renal AKI with a raised urea:creatinine ratio. Rehydration usually reverses it; monitor U&E closely.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What is cyclical vomiting syndrome / how does cannabinoid hyperemesis present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Recurrent, stereotyped episodes of severe vomiting with symptom-free intervals. Cannabinoid hyperemesis is a variant in chronic cannabis users, classically relieved by hot showers / baths and by stopping cannabis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: How does raised intracranial pressure produce vomiting?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: It stimulates the area postrema (which sits in the floor of the fourth ventricle) and the medullary vomiting centre — often producing projectile vomiting, classically without preceding nausea, with headache and papilloedema.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What bloods are useful in the initial work-up of significant vomiting?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
• U&E (AKI, K⁺, alkalosis)
  • glucose & ketones
  • calcium
  • amylase / lipase
  • LFTs
  • and a VBG
— plus a βhCG in women and an ECG.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Why does hypercalcaemia cause vomiting, and what else does it cause?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: High calcium reduces neuromuscular / GI excitability and stimulates the CTZ — causing nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, confusion and stones (‘bones, stones, groans, moans’). Check calcium in unexplained vomiting.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What is the significance of vomiting with abdominal distension and absolute constipation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: It is the picture of bowel obstruction — colicky pain, distension, vomiting (bilious then faeculent) and no flatus. Manage with NBM, IV fluids and an NG tube, and image (AXR / CT).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Does the sequence of pain and vomiting help localise the cause?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Pain before vomiting favours a surgical cause (e.g. appendicitis, obstruction); vomiting before pain favours a medical cause such as gastroenteritis — a useful history discriminator.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What are the risks of vomiting in a patient with a reduced conscious level?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Aspiration of gastric contents → aspiration pneumonia / pneumonitis and airway compromise. Protect the airway (recovery position / definitive airway), and consider an NG tube for decompression.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: What safe-prescribing cautions apply to common antiemetics (MHRA)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back:
• Ondansetron — QT prolongation (avoid with a long QT or other QT-prolonging drugs)
  • domperidone — cardiac / QT risk (lowest dose, short course, avoid in cardiac disease)
  • metoclopramide — maximum 5-day course because of extrapyramidal effects.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Which antiemetic is preferred in Parkinson's disease, and which are avoided?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Domperidone is preferred — it antagonises D₂ peripherally but crosses the blood-brain barrier minimally, so it does not worsen Parkinsonism. Avoid metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and haloperidol (central D₂ antagonists). Cyclizine and ondansetron are also safe.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.front: Why give thiamine to a patient with protracted vomiting or hyperemesis gravidarum?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiti.back: Prolonged vomiting with poor intake risks thiamine (B1) deficiency and Wernicke’s encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) — which a glucose load can precipitate. Replace thiamine before or with glucose in at-risk patients.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is PR (rectal) bleeding, and what does it usually indicate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Blood passed per rectum (haematochezia) — usually a lower-GI source (distal to the ligament of Treitz). This contrasts with melaena (black, tarry — an upper-GI bleed).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How does the colour of PR blood help localise the source?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Bright red → anorectal / distal colon; darker / plum → more proximal colon; maroon or brisk red → a right-colon source or a rapid upper-GI bleed. Colour alone is a guide, not proof.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What does the relation of blood to the stool tell you?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Blood on the paper, coating the stool, or dripping suggests an outlet / anorectal source (haemorrhoids, fissure). Blood mixed through the stool suggests a colonic source (cancer, IBD, diverticular).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How do haemorrhoids typically cause PR bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Painless, bright red bleeding on the paper, coating the stool, or dripping into the pan — often with straining / constipation. Confirmed on proctoscopy; treated with fibre / fluids, topical measures, banding or surgery.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How does an anal fissure present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Painful defecation with bright red blood on the paper and a hard stool — a tear usually in the posterior midline. Treated with stool softeners, high fibre and topical GTN or diltiazem to relax the sphincter.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is the commonest cause of acute, brisk lower-GI haemorrhage?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Diverticular bleeding — a brisk, painless bleed (an eroded vessel in a diverticulum), usually in an older patient. It usually stops spontaneously; CT angiography / colonoscopy localise it if it does not.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is angiodysplasia, and who gets it?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Fragile, dilated submucosal vessels (often right colon) causing recurrent, painless PR bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia in the elderly. Diagnosed at colonoscopy / angiography; treated with endoscopic ablation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is Heyde's syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: The association of aortic stenosis + GI angiodysplasia bleeding, mediated by an acquired von Willebrand deficiency (vWF is destroyed by turbulent flow across the stenotic valve). Aortic valve replacement can resolve the bleeding.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How does colorectal cancer present with PR bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Blood mixed in with the stool, with a change in bowel habit, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia or tenesmus (rectal tumour) — especially in the older patient. Investigate with FIT and colonoscopy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: Why must rectal bleeding in an older patient never be attributed to haemorrhoids without investigation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Because colorectal cancer is common and can coexist with haemorrhoids — a new change of bowel habit, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, a mass, or age ≥50 with rectal bleeding needs colonoscopy on the suspected-cancer pathway.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How does inflammatory bowel disease present with PR bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency and abdominal pain in a younger patient, often with weight loss and a raised faecal calprotectin. Colonoscopy with biopsy confirms ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: Which infective organisms cause bloody diarrhoea (infective colitis)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back:
• Campylobacter
  • Shigella
  • Salmonella
  • E. coli O157
  • and Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery)
— consider recent travel, food and antibiotics; send stool culture (and remember C. difficile).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How does ischaemic colitis present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Sudden crampy abdominal pain (often left-sided) followed by bloody diarrhoea in an older patient with vascular risk factors — from reduced colonic perfusion (splenic-flexure watershed). Usually managed supportively.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is radiation proctitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Rectal bleeding, urgency and tenesmus occurring months to years after pelvic radiotherapy (e.g. for prostate / gynaecological cancer) — from telangiectasia and mucosal damage; treated endoscopically (e.g. argon plasma coagulation).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is the classic cause of painless PR bleeding in a young child?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: A Meckel’s diverticulum — ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid causing painless PR bleeding (the ‘rule of 2s’: 2% of people, 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long). Diagnosed with a technetium (Meckel’s) scan.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How is an acute, severe lower-GI bleed managed initially?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back:
ABCDE resuscitation —
  • two large-bore cannulae
  • bloods including group & crossmatch
  • IV fluids / blood
  • the major haemorrhage protocol if massive
  • and correction of any coagulopathy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: Why should a brisk UPPER-GI bleed be considered in severe 'PR bleeding'?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: A rapid upper-GI bleed can pass as fresh / maroon blood per rectum (fast transit) — and up to ~15% of presumed lower-GI bleeds are actually upper. If the patient is unstable with no lower source, do an OGD before assuming a colonic origin.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is the role of CT angiography in lower-GI bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: In an acute, actively bleeding patient it localises the bleeding point (and can guide embolisation). It is used when bleeding is too brisk for colonoscopy or the patient is unstable after resuscitation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is the role of colonoscopy in PR bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: The mainstay for stable patients — it visualises the colon, biopsies lesions, removes polyps and can treat bleeding points. It is the definitive investigation for suspected cancer, IBD, and recurrent bleeding.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What examination should never be omitted in PR bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: A digital rectal examination and proctoscopy — to identify haemorrhoids, an anal fissure or a low rectal mass, and to see the character of the blood. It is essential before attributing bleeding to a benign cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: Which bedside / blood tests are used in PR bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back:
• Observations (for shock)
  • FBC (anaemia)
  • U&E
  • LFTs, clotting and group & save / crossmatch
plus FIT and stool tests as appropriate.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is the significance of tenesmus with PR bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Tenesmus (a sensation of incomplete evacuation) with rectal bleeding suggests a rectal mass / cancer or proctitis — a localising red flag prompting urgent examination and colonoscopy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How are internal haemorrhoids graded and managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back:
• 1st degree (no prolapse)
  • 2nd (prolapse, reduce spontaneously)
  • 3rd (need manual reduction)
  • 4th (irreducible).
Manage with fibre / fluids and topical measures, then banding, with surgery (haemorrhoidectomy) for high-grade / refractory disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What score risk-stratifies acute lower-GI bleeding, and what does it decide?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: The Oakland score (age, sex, previous bleed, PR-exam findings, heart rate, systolic BP, haemoglobin). A low score (≤8) identifies patients suitable for safe outpatient management; higher scores need admission (BSG/ACPGBI 2019). Note Blatchford/Rockall are for upper-GI bleeds.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How does the FIT test guide referral in PR bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: A faecal immunochemical test detects occult blood; a result ≥10 µg Hb/g faeces triggers urgent colonoscopy on the suspected-cancer pathway. But visible rectal bleeding with red flags warrants referral regardless, and a negative FIT does not exclude cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What distinguishes proctitis as a cause of PR bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Inflammation limited to the rectum — causing bleeding, mucus, urgency and tenesmus. Causes include ulcerative proctitis (IBD), infective / sexually-transmitted proctitis, and radiation; diagnosed on sigmoidoscopy + biopsy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: Why can PR bleeding cause iron-deficiency anaemia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Chronic slow blood loss (e.g. from a right-sided cancer, angiodysplasia or polyps) depletes iron over time — presenting as iron-deficiency anaemia, which itself is a red flag mandating GI investigation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is a useful discriminator between an upper- and lower-GI source of PR blood?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: A raised urea (out of proportion to creatinine) and melaena / haematemesis favour an upper-GI source (digested blood); bright red blood mixed with or coating formed stool, with a normal urea, favours a lower-GI source.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How is a diverticular bleed managed if it does not stop spontaneously?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Resuscitate, then CT angiography to localise it (± radiological embolisation), or colonoscopic haemostasis; segmental colectomy is reserved for uncontrolled or recurrent bleeding.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What causes should be considered for painless, large-volume PR bleeding in an older adult?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: Diverticular bleeding (commonest) and angiodysplasia — both brisk and painless. Colorectal cancer and a brisk upper-GI bleed must also be excluded; ischaemic colitis is usually painful.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: How are anticoagulants and antiplatelets handled in significant lower-GI bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back:
• Warfarin → hold and reverse with IV vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
  • dabigatran → idarucizumab
  • factor-Xa inhibitors → PCC (± andexanet).
Weigh thrombotic risk before stopping antiplatelets. Tranexamic acid is NOT routine in GI bleeding (no benefit, more VTE).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is the classic 'can't-miss' cause of massive PR bleeding after aortic surgery?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: An aorto-enteric fistula — suspect in anyone with a previous open AAA / aortic-graft repair who has a small 'herald' GI bleed then catastrophic haemorrhage. Needs urgent CT angiography and vascular / surgical input; a missed diagnosis is rapidly fatal.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What haemoglobin transfusion threshold is used in acute GI bleeding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: A restrictive strategy (NICE): transfuse red cells at Hb <70 g/L, targeting 70–90 g/L — unless the patient has haemodynamic instability or cardiovascular disease (use a higher threshold of ~80). Over-transfusion worsens outcomes in variceal / GI bleeds.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.front: What is solitary rectal ulcer syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding.back: A rare cause of PR bleeding in younger adults with chronic straining or rectal prolapse — presenting with rectal bleeding, mucus, tenesmus and a sensation of incomplete evacuation. Sigmoidoscopy shows a solitary anterior-rectal ulcer; managed with fibre, fluids and biofeedback (behavioural bowel retraining).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What is odynophagia, and how does it differ from dysphagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Odynophagia = pain on swallowing; dysphagia = difficulty swallowing. They often coexist, but odynophagia specifically points to inflammation or ulceration of the swallowing tract (an ‘-algia’ of swallowing).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: How do you localise painful swallowing to the oropharynx versus the oesophagus?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Oropharyngeal: a sore throat with pain at the start of the swallow (tonsillitis, ulcers, quinsy). Oesophageal: retrosternal pain a few seconds after swallowing (oesophagitis, ulcer, tumour).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What is the commonest cause category of oesophageal odynophagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back:
Oesophagitis —
  • infective (Candida, HSV, CMV)
  • pill / chemical (bisphosphonates, doxycycline, caustics)
  • or severe reflux (erosive) oesophagitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What are the risk factors for oesophageal candidiasis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back:
Immunosuppression —
  • HIV / AIDS
  • chemotherapy
  • corticosteroids (including inhaled)
  • diabetes
  • and recent broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Oral thrush is often visible alongside it.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: How is oesophageal candidiasis diagnosed and treated in an immunocompromised patient with odynophagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: With oral thrush and odynophagia, treat empirically with oral fluconazole — endoscopy is reserved for no response. On OGD it shows white mucosal plaques.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What are the endoscopic features of HSV versus CMV oesophagitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: HSV: multiple small, shallow ‘punched-out’ ulcers / vesicles. CMV: large, deep, solitary ulcers. Both indicate significant immunosuppression (e.g. AIDS, transplant); biopsy shows the viral inclusions.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What is pill (medication) oesophagitis and which drugs cause it?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Direct mucosal injury from a tablet lodging in the oesophagus — classically bisphosphonates, doxycycline / tetracyclines, NSAIDs, potassium and iron, taken with too little water or while lying down.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: How is pill oesophagitis prevented?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Take culprit tablets sitting or standing upright, with a full glass of water, and remain upright for 30 minutes afterwards. Stopping / substituting the drug allows the mucosa to heal.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: How does caustic (corrosive) oesophagitis present and what must you NOT do?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: After acid / alkali ingestion (accidental or deliberate) — oral / retrosternal pain, drooling, odynophagia. Do NOT induce vomiting or blindly pass an NG tube; get senior help and endoscopic assessment. Alkalis cause deep liquefactive injury.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: Which airway emergencies can present with severe painful swallowing?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Epiglottitis, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) and deep-neck-space infections — suspect if the patient cannot swallow saliva (drooling), is febrile, with a muffled voice or stridor. Call the airway team.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What are the features of acute epiglottitis, and the key rule?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Rapid-onset severe sore throat, drooling, a muffled ‘hot-potato’ voice, the tripod position and stridor, often febrile and toxic. Do NOT examine the throat / distress a child — secure the airway (ENT / anaesthetics). Classically caused by H. influenzae type b.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What are the features of a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Unilateral severe throat pain and odynophagia, trismus (difficulty opening the mouth), a ‘hot-potato’ voice, and deviation of the uvula away from the swollen tonsil. Treated with drainage and antibiotics.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: Why should amoxicillin be avoided in suspected glandular fever (EBV)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: It classically causes a widespread maculopapular rash in EBV infectious mononucleosis. Glandular fever gives sore throat, odynophagia, fever, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly — avoid contact sport (splenic rupture risk).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What is the first investigation for unexplained or refractory OESOPHAGEAL odynophagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Upper-GI endoscopy (OGD) with biopsy / brushings — to identify infective oesophagitis (Candida / HSV / CMV), pill injury, or an ulcerating tumour, and to obtain tissue / microbiology.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: Why should an HIV test be considered in a patient with oesophageal candidiasis or viral oesophagitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Oesophageal candidiasis is an AIDS-defining illness, and HSV / CMV oesophagitis implies significant immunosuppression — these may be the presenting feature of undiagnosed HIV. Check an HIV test and CD4 count.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: How does erosive reflux oesophagitis cause odynophagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Severe acid reflux inflames and ulcerates the lower-oesophageal mucosa, adding pain on swallowing to the usual heartburn. It is treated with a PPI (and it can cause strictures and Barrett’s over time).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What causes odynophagia in a patient recently treated with chemotherapy or radiotherapy?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Mucositis — direct injury to the oral / oesophageal mucosa (and neutropenia predisposing to infective oesophagitis, esp. Candida). Management is supportive (analgesia, oral care, nutrition) plus treating any infection.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What is oral candidiasis (thrush) and what does its presence suggest with odynophagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: White, wipeable plaques on the oral mucosa leaving a raw base. With odynophagia it strongly suggests oesophageal candidiasis — and prompts a search for immunosuppression (HIV, steroids, diabetes).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What are aphthous ulcers, and when should recurrent ones prompt further thought?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Small, painful, shallow oral ulcers with a grey base and red halo. Usually benign / idiopathic, but recurrent or severe ulcers can point to coeliac disease, IBD, Behçet’s or immunodeficiency.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: How is viral (HSV or CMV) oesophagitis treated?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back:
• HSV oesophagitis → aciclovir
  • CMV oesophagitis → ganciclovir / valganciclovir (foscarnet if resistant or intolerant).
Alongside, treat the underlying immunosuppression — e.g. start / optimise antiretroviral therapy in HIV.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What ominous cause must progressive odynophagia with weight loss suggest?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: An ulcerating oesophageal cancer — progressive painful swallowing with weight loss (± dysphagia, anaemia) in an older patient needs urgent OGD with biopsy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: Which single question best triages the safety of a patient with severe painful swallowing?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: “Can you swallow your own saliva?” — drooling / inability to swallow saliva (with fever, muffled voice or stridor) signals a threatened airway (epiglottitis / quinsy / deep-neck infection).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: How is glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis) confirmed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: A monospot / heterophile antibody test (and EBV serology); blood film shows atypical lymphocytes. Caused by EBV; supportive treatment, avoid amoxicillin and contact sports (splenic rupture).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What examination findings accompany bacterial tonsillitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back:
• Fever
  • enlarged erythematous tonsils with exudate
  • tender cervical lymphadenopathy
  • and odynophagia.
The CENTOR / FeverPAIN criteria guide whether antibiotics are appropriate.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: Why is odynophagia in an inhaled-corticosteroid user a clue?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Inhaled steroids predispose to oral and oesophageal candidiasis (local immunosuppression) — a common, easily-missed cause; advise rinsing the mouth / using a spacer after inhaler use.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What is the difference in mucosal injury between acid and alkali ingestion?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Alkalis cause deep liquefactive necrosis (penetrating, higher perforation / stricture risk); acids cause coagulative necrosis (a more superficial eschar). Both need senior and endoscopic assessment.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What supportive measures matter in any patient with significant odynophagia?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Adequate analgesia, hydration and nutrition (the pain limits oral intake) — consider soft / liquid diet, and IV fluids or alternative feeding if intake is inadequate, alongside treating the cause.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: How does the timing of pain within the swallow help localise the cause?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Pain immediately, at the start of the swallow suggests an oropharyngeal cause (tonsils, pharynx); pain a few seconds later, felt retrosternally suggests an oesophageal cause (oesophagitis, ulcer, tumour).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: What long-term oesophageal complications can follow caustic or severe oesophagitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: Strictures (causing later dysphagia), and, after caustic injury, a long-term increased risk of oesophageal squamous carcinoma — so follow-up and surveillance may be needed.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.front: Which infective oesophagitis is most associated with very advanced immunosuppression (low CD4)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Painful Swallow.back: CMV oesophagitis (large deep ulcers) typically occurs at very low CD4 counts in AIDS or transplant patients; Candida occurs at higher CD4 than CMV/HSV but still signals immunosuppression.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: What is palmar erythema and where is it seen?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Symmetrical redness of the palms over the thenar and hypothenar eminences (and finger pulps), classically sparing the central palm. It is warm and blanches on pressure, and is usually bilateral and asymptomatic.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: What is the mechanism of palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Relative oestrogen excess causing cutaneous vasodilatation — the same mechanism as spider naevi (so the two commonly coexist). It reflects a hyperdynamic / high-oestrogen state rather than being specific to the liver.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Why is palmar erythema described as a 'soft' sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Because it is non-specific — it occurs in health (familial, pregnancy) and in several diseases. Its value depends on context: with spider naevi and other stigmata it supports chronic liver disease, but alone it may be normal.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Which physiological states cause palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Pregnancy and the combined oral contraceptive pill (oestrogen-driven), and a familial / hereditary variant that is lifelong and benign; it can also be a normal finding in healthy people.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: What is the most important pathological cause of palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Chronic liver disease (cirrhosis, especially alcohol-related) — via impaired hepatic oestrogen metabolism; look for the other stigmata (spider naevi, leukonychia, gynaecomastia, Dupuytren’s, jaundice, ascites).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Which endocrine condition causes palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Thyrotoxicosis (hyperthyroidism) — through a hyperdynamic circulation, alongside warm moist skin, tremor, weight loss and heat intolerance.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Which haematological conditions cause palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Polycythaemia (plethora, aquagenic pruritus, raised haematocrit) and chronic leukaemia — hyperviscosity / hyperdynamic states.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Which rheumatological condition is associated with palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Rheumatoid arthritis — a recognised association (along with other connective-tissue disease); look for symmetrical small-joint arthritis and deformity.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Which hand / skin signs cluster together in alcohol-related liver disease?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Palmar erythema, Dupuytren’s contracture and spider naevi (with leukonychia and gynaecomastia) classically cluster in alcohol-related liver disease — a favourite examination combination.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: How can you tell palmar erythema from a scaly palmar dermatosis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Palmar erythema is smooth, blanching redness without scale or itch; eczema and psoriasis give scaly, itchy or fissured palms (psoriasis with nail pitting / onycholysis) — a different, textured rash.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Is palmar erythema itself harmful, and how is it managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: It is harmless in itself (a cosmetic / diagnostic sign); management is directed at the underlying cause. An isolated, lifelong, familial finding needs only reassurance.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: What other stigmata should you look for when you find palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back:
The full set of chronic-liver-disease stigmata:
  • spider naevi
  • leukonychia
  • gynaecomastia
  • Dupuytren’s contracture
  • clubbing
  • jaundice
  • caput medusae
  • ascites and asterixis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: What investigations are appropriate for new symmetrical palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: A full chronic-liver-disease examination, then LFTs, clotting and FBC; add TFTs, a pregnancy test and a rheumatological assessment as the history suggests.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Does palmar erythema resolve?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Physiological forms regress (e.g. after pregnancy or stopping the oestrogen), and cause-related erythema may improve when the underlying disease is treated; the familial (Lane’s) form is permanent.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: What features distinguish palmar erythema from other red / painful palms?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: It is painless, non-tender, warm and blanching (not permanently red) — unlike cellulitis (tender, hot, spreading) or erythromelalgia (burning pain, worse with warmth). The central palm is relatively spared.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: How does the finding of palmar erythema change with the disease that causes it?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: It is non-specific and does not indicate severity on its own; interpret it alongside the other findings. In liver disease it accompanies (and rises with) the other oestrogen-mediated stigmata.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: What blood test rapidly supports polycythaemia as a cause of palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: A full blood count showing a raised haemoglobin / haematocrit — with plethora and aquagenic pruritus; confirm and subtype (e.g. JAK2 for polycythaemia vera).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Which conditions should always be considered in the differential of palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back:
• Chronic liver disease
  • pregnancy / the OCP
  • thyrotoxicosis
  • rheumatoid arthritis
  • polycythaemia
  • diabetes and a familial / normal variant
— a genuinely cross-system list.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: What is the name for the inherited form of palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Erythema palmare hereditarium (Lane’s disease) — a benign, lifelong, autosomal-dominant palmar erythema present in otherwise-well family members; recognising it avoids unnecessary investigation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Why does palmar erythema occur in a hyperdynamic circulation?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: States with increased cutaneous blood flow / vasodilatation — thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, fever, and chronic liver disease — produce the warm, blanching palmar redness; it is a vascular, not an inflammatory, sign.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Is palmar erythema usually symmetrical or unilateral?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Symmetrical (bilateral) — a systemic / vascular cause is implied. A unilateral red palm suggests a local cause (trauma, infection, contact dermatitis) rather than the classic systemic sign.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Does diabetes cause palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: It is a recognised but weaker association — diabetes mellitus is listed among the systemic causes of palmar erythema, alongside the (stronger) liver, endocrine, rheumatological and haematological causes.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: How does erythromelalgia differ from palmar erythema?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Erythromelalgia causes burning pain with red, hot extremities, triggered by warmth and relieved by cooling (associated with myeloproliferative disease). Palmar erythema is painless, warm and blanching — a key discriminator.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.front: Which liver diseases can underlie palmar erythema besides alcohol?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Palmar Erythema.back: Any cause of chronic liver disease / cirrhosis — non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, chronic viral hepatitis, haemochromatosis and Wilson’s disease — all can produce the oestrogen-mediated stigmata.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is peritonism?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: The clinical signs of an irritated parietal peritoneum — guarding, rigidity, rebound / percussion tenderness and pain worse on movement or coughing. It is peritonitis as detected on examination.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: Why does the parietal peritoneum localise pain sharply while visceral pain is vague?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: The parietal peritoneum has a somatic nerve supply, so irritation gives sharp, well-localised, movement-sensitive pain. The visceral peritoneum / organs have autonomic afferents, giving dull, poorly localised, midline pain.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is the difference between voluntary and involuntary guarding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back:
• Voluntary guarding is anticipatory tensing the patient can suppress (with distraction, warm hands, gentle technique)
  • Involuntary guarding is a reflex contraction they cannot override — it is the hallmark of true peritonism

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is meant by a 'board-like rigid' abdomen?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Sustained, generalised involuntary guarding — the abdominal wall is hard and immobile. It is the most extreme, ominous sign of peritonism and suggests generalised peritonitis (e.g. perforation).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is rebound tenderness (Blumberg's sign)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Pain that is worse on the sudden release of deep palpation than on pressing in — the peritoneum rebounds against the inflamed surface. It indicates peritoneal irritation but is crude and unkind.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: Why is percussion tenderness preferred over testing for rebound?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Percussion tenderness (and the cough test) demonstrate peritoneal irritation just as reliably but are gentler and more humane — hard rebound testing causes unnecessary pain and is now discouraged.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is the cough test in the abdominal examination?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Asking the patient to cough; if it produces sharp, localised abdominal pain, it signifies peritoneal irritation — a gentle screen for peritonism before you even palpate.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: Why does a patient with peritonitis lie completely still, unlike a patient with colic?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: In peritonitis, any movement, coughing or jolting (even the car journey in) stretches the inflamed peritoneum and hurts, so the patient lies rigidly still. In colic (e.g. a ureteric stone) the pain is not movement-related, so the patient is instead restless and writhing.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is Rovsing's sign and what does it suggest?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Palpating the LEFT iliac fossa produces pain in the RIGHT iliac fossa — suggestive of appendicitis (localised RIF peritoneal irritation).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is the psoas sign and when is it positive?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Pain on passive extension (or active flexion) of the right hip, from irritation of the psoas muscle by an inflamed retrocaecal appendix — a clue when the abdomen itself seems relatively soft.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is the obturator sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed right hip, from an inflamed pelvic appendix irritating the obturator internus — another localising sign in appendicitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is Murphy's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: During RUQ palpation, the patient catches their breath (arrests inspiration) as the inflamed gallbladder descends onto your hand — localised biliary peritonism indicating acute cholecystitis. It should be negative on the left.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What does cervical excitation (cervical motion tenderness) indicate?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Pain on moving the cervix on bimanual examination signifies pelvic peritoneal irritation — e.g. pelvic inflammatory disease or ectopic pregnancy. Always do a βhCG.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is Carnett's sign and how is it used?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: With the tender spot identified, the patient tenses the abdominal wall (lifts head or legs). If tenderness increases, the pain is in the abdominal wall (Carnett’s positive); if it decreases, it is intra-abdominal / peritoneal.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is the clinical importance of distinguishing localised from generalised peritonism?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back:
• Localised peritonism points to a single inflamed organ (appendix, gallbladder, diverticulum) — often treatable in a targeted way
  • Generalised peritonism means spillage / perforation — a surgical emergency

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What causes generalised (secondary) peritonitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back:
Spillage into the peritoneal cavity —
  • a perforated viscus (ulcer, diverticulum, appendix)
  • ischaemic / dead bowel
  • or leakage of pus, bile, blood or bowel content

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: Why does the abdomen become silent (absent bowel sounds) in peritonitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: The inflamed gut stops contracting, producing a paralytic ileus — hence a tense, still, silent abdomen. It is an important accompanying sign of generalised peritonitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is the difference between primary and secondary peritonitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back:
• Primary (spontaneous) peritonitis is infection of the peritoneal fluid without a perforation (e.g. SBP in ascites)
  • Secondary peritonitis follows a breach / perforation of the GI tract and usually needs surgery

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: How is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) diagnosed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: In a patient with ascites (usually cirrhotic), an ascitic tap showing neutrophils ≥250 cells/mm³ is diagnostic. It is treated with antibiotics — not surgery — and is a form of primary peritonitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: In which patients may peritoneal signs be blunted or absent despite serious pathology?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back:
• The elderly
  • immunosuppressed
  • those on steroids
  • diabetics
  • and pregnant women
— the guarding / rigidity may be muted, so serious disease is under-called. Keep a low threshold for imaging.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: How is generalised peritonism managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back:
• Resuscitate (ABCDE, NBM, IV access, fluids, analgesia, bloods incl. lactate & βhCG)
  • give broad-spectrum antibiotics if septic
  • and call surgery
— the likely need is a laparotomy for source control.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is McBurney's point and its significance?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: The point two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine — maximal tenderness here reflects localised parietal peritonism over the inflamed appendix.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: Is shifting dullness a sign of peritonism?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: No. Shifting dullness indicates ascites (free fluid), not peritoneal irritation. Peritonism is shown by guarding, rigidity and rebound / percussion tenderness — do not confuse the two.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: Why can a lower-lobe pneumonia cause upper abdominal guarding?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Diaphragmatic pleural irritation refers to the upper abdomen and can produce guarding that mimics peritonism. Always examine the chest — a basal pneumonia is a classic non-surgical mimic.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What percussion sign at the bedside suggests free intraperitoneal air (perforation)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Loss of the normal liver dullness to percussion over the lower right ribs — a layer of free gas (pneumoperitoneum) from a perforated viscus sits over the liver. An erect chest X-ray then confirms free air under the diaphragm.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What is the sonographic Murphy's sign?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Maximal tenderness elicited as the ultrasound probe is pressed directly over the gallbladder during scanning. Combined with a thick-walled gallbladder and stones, it is more specific than the clinical Murphy’s sign for acute cholecystitis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What accompanying observations suggest peritonism has become a surgical emergency?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Generalised rigidity, a silent abdomen, and systemic signs of shock / sepsis (tachycardia, hypotension, fever, oliguria) — together they point to generalised peritonitis needing urgent surgery.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: Why must a woman of reproductive age with lower-abdominal peritonism have a βhCG?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: To exclude an ectopic pregnancy — pelvic peritonism with a positive βhCG and instability is a surgical emergency. Ectopic and PID are key causes of pelvic peritoneal signs.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: Besides lying still, what inspection sign points to generalised peritonitis?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: A rigid abdomen that does not move with respiration — normally the abdominal wall rises and falls with breathing, but with peritonitis the patient splints it and breathes shallowly with the chest to avoid moving the inflamed peritoneum.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: How does generalised peritonitis lead to shock?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Inflamed peritoneum weeps fluid into the abdomen (third-spacing) and drives a systemic inflammatory / septic response — causing hypovolaemia and distributive shock. This is why aggressive resuscitation is needed alongside surgery.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: Why may a retrocaecal appendix produce few abdominal signs?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: The inflamed appendix lies behind the caecum, away from the anterior parietal peritoneum, so guarding may be minimal — the psoas sign and localised deep tenderness become the key clues.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: How can you tell that guarding is involuntary rather than voluntary?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back: Involuntary guarding persists despite distraction, warm hands, gentle technique and asking the patient to relax with knees bent — it is a reflex that cannot be suppressed, and it is the hallmark of true peritonism. Voluntary guarding eases with these manoeuvres.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: Describe the humane sequence for eliciting peritonism.
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back:
• Inspect (does the patient lie still?)
  • use the cough test
  • then light palpation for guarding and gentle percussion tenderness
— warm hands, watch the face, and start away from the pain. Reserve deep rebound testing.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.front: What examinations complete the assessment of an acute peritonitic abdomen?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Gua.back:
• Examine all hernial orifices
  • perform a PR examination
  • do a pelvic exam / βhCG in women
  • and examine the chest (basal pneumonia mimic)
— alongside the peritoneal signs themselves.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How do you approach rectal pain and a perianal lump at the bedside?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Characterise the pain (severe on defecation → fissure; constant throbbing + fever → abscess; sudden acutely painful lump → thrombosed pile) and the lump (position, tenderness, reducibility, discharge). Then split the acutely painful trio from chronic lumps, and exclude sepsis and cancer.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How does a perianal abscess present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Constant, throbbing perianal pain with a hot, tender, fluctuant swelling, worse on sitting, often with fever. It is a collection of pus needing surgical incision & drainage — the commonest anorectal surgical emergency.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is the correct treatment of a perianal abscess?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Urgent incision & drainage (usually examination under anaesthesia) — antibiotics alone will not cure it. Antibiotics are adjuncts for surrounding cellulitis, diabetes or immunosuppression, or systemic sepsis.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is Fournier's gangrene and who is at risk?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Necrotising fasciitis of the perineum / genitalia — a surgical emergency in diabetic or immunocompromised patients. Suspect it with pain out of proportion, crepitus, necrosis or systemic sepsis; treat with resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and immediate debridement.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How does an anal fissure present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Severe, sharp / tearing pain on defecation (like 'passing glass'), often lasting hours afterwards, with bright red blood on the paper. A chronic fissure has a sentinel skin tag; most are in the posterior midline.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How is an anal fissure managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Stool softeners, high fibre and fluids plus topical GTN or diltiazem (relax the internal sphincter). If it fails: botulinum toxin or lateral internal sphincterotomy (small risk of incontinence).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How does a thrombosed external haemorrhoid (perianal haematoma) present, and how is it managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: A sudden, exquisitely tender, tense blue / purple lump at the anal verge. If it presents within ~72 hours, consider excision for rapid relief; later, manage conservatively (analgesia, softeners, ice) as it resolves over 1–2 weeks.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How are internal haemorrhoids graded?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back:
• 1st degree — no prolapse
  • 2nd — prolapse on straining, reduce spontaneously
  • 3rd — prolapse, need manual reduction
  • 4th — irreducible (permanently prolapsed, may strangulate).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How does management of haemorrhoids vary by grade?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back:
• Conservative (fibre, fluids, topical) for all — and alone for 1st degree
  • rubber-band ligation for symptomatic 2nd–3rd degree
  • haemorrhoidectomy or stapled / HALO procedures for 3rd–4th degree or refractory disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: Why are internal haemorrhoids usually painless but external ones painful?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back:
The dentate (pectinate) line divides the anal canal:
  • above it is insensate visceral mucosa (internal haemorrhoids — painless)
  • below it is somatically innervated (external haemorrhoids / thrombosis — painful).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is a fistula-in-ano?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: An abnormal track between the anal canal and the perianal skin, usually following a previous perianal abscess. It presents with a persistently discharging perianal opening and recurrent abscesses; recurrent or complex disease may be the first presentation of Crohn’s.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is Goodsall's rule?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: It predicts a fistula track: an external opening anterior to the transverse anal line tends to track radially / straight to the anal canal; a posterior opening tends to curve to the posterior midline.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How is a fistula-in-ano managed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Define the track (clinical ± MRI pelvis / EUA), then lay open a simple low fistula (fistulotomy); for high / complex tracks use a seton to preserve the sphincter and drain sepsis. Exclude Crohn’s disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is pilonidal disease?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: A sinus / abscess in the natal cleft (containing hair and debris), typically in young, hairy men. It presents with a painful discharging swelling; managed by drainage of any abscess, then excision / definitive surgery and hygiene / hair control.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How does rectal prolapse present, and in whom?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Full-thickness protrusion of the rectum through the anus (concentric mucosal rings), often with mucus, bleeding and faecal incontinence. Seen in elderly women (pelvic-floor weakness) and in children (associated with straining / cystic fibrosis).

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What are the features of perianal Crohn's disease?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Complex or multiple fistulae, recurrent abscesses, skin tags and fissures that are often lateral or multiple (not the usual posterior midline) — with diarrhoea and weight loss. It signals Crohn’s and needs colonoscopy + MRI.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What type of cancer is anal cancer and what are its risk factors?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back:
Most anal cancers are squamous cell carcinomas driven by HPV (16/18). Risk factors:
  • HPV infection
  • HIV / immunosuppression
  • receptive anal intercourse
  • smoking and a history of anogenital dysplasia.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How does anal cancer present?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: A hard, irregular, non-healing anal mass or ulcer with pain, bleeding, pruritus or tenesmus, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Any non-healing perianal lesion warrants biopsy and suspected-cancer referral.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How is anal (squamous cell) cancer treated?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Chemoradiotherapy (the Nigro regimen — mitomycin, 5-FU + radiotherapy) is first-line and often sphincter-preserving; salvage surgery (abdominoperineal resection) is reserved for residual / recurrent disease.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How does low rectal cancer differ from anal cancer?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Rectal cancer is usually adenocarcinoma (palpable mass on DRE, tenesmus, bleeding, change in bowel habit) staged and often resected; anal cancer is usually squamous and treated primarily with chemoradiotherapy.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is proctalgia fugax?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: A functional disorder of fleeting, severe cramping rectal pain (seconds to minutes, often at night) with a normal examination. It is benign, but organic causes must be excluded first; reassurance ± measures like warmth or GTN help.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is levator ani syndrome?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Chronic or recurrent dull rectal / pelvic-floor ache (worse sitting) from levator-ani muscle tension, with a normal structural examination. Managed with reassurance, physiotherapy / biofeedback and muscle relaxation.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What causes pruritus ani, and how is it approached?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back:
Perianal itch — often idiopathic, or from
  • haemorrhoids
  • skin tags
  • threadworms
  • fungal / contact dermatitis
  • poor or over-hygiene
  • or diabetes.
Treat the cause, optimise hygiene, and exclude neoplasia in persistent cases.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: Which organism causes anogenital warts?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Human papillomavirus (HPV), usually types 6 and 11 (low-risk) — causing condylomata acuminata. Types 16/18 are the oncogenic ones linked to anal cancer; consider an STI / HIV screen.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is the essential examination in rectal pain / a perianal lump?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: Inspection of the perianal skin (clock-face position), digital rectal examination and proctoscopy — to characterise the lump, feel for a mass and assess sphincter tone.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: When is examination under anaesthesia (EUA) needed?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: When the area is too painful to examine awake (e.g. fissure, abscess), to drain an abscess, to define a fistula track, or to biopsy a suspicious mass — it allows a full, pain-free assessment and treatment.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is the role of MRI pelvis in perianal disease?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: MRI pelvis is the best test to map fistula tracks and complex / recurrent sepsis and to assess perianal Crohn’s — it guides surgery (seton vs lay-open) and detects deep collections. Endoanal ultrasound is an alternative for track and sphincter assessment.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is a sentinel pile (skin tag)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: A skin tag at the distal end of a chronic anal fissure (or after a haemorrhoid). It is a marker of chronicity; the tag itself is benign but points to the underlying fissure that needs treating.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is anal intraepithelial neoplasia (AIN)?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: HPV-driven dysplasia of the anal squamous epithelium — the precursor to anal squamous cell carcinoma. Risk is highest in HIV-positive men who have sex with men; it may be screened with anal cytology / high-resolution anoscopy and treated to prevent progression.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: How are anorectal abscesses classified by anatomical space?
signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.back: By the space involved: perianal (commonest, superficial at the verge), ischiorectal (deeper fossa — deep buttock pain, less visible swelling, more systemic upset), and the deeper intersphincteric and supralevator abscesses (may need imaging to find). All need surgical drainage.

signs__GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / P.front: What is solitary rectal ulcer syndrome?
